DateTime::from_second(seconds: i64)Result<DateTime, jiff::Error>seconds since the Unix epoch
DateTime::from_millisecond(milliseconds: i64)Result<DateTime, jiff::Error>milliseconds since the Unix epoch
DateTime::from_microsecond(microseconds: i64)Result<DateTime, jiff::Error>microseconds since the Unix epoch
DateTime::from_nanosecond(nanoseconds: i128)Result<DateTime, jiff::Error>nanoseconds since the Unix epoch
DateTime::from_duration(duration: jiff::SignedDuration)Result<DateTime, jiff::Error>epoch-relative duration
DateTime::now()DateTimereads the system clock; not const

The constructor names mirror the underlying time library verbatim; they are not invented. Names that do not exist on DateTime and will not be added: from_unix_timestamp, from_unix_nanos.

Each from_* constructor returns a Result and propagates an out-of-range argument as the underlying time library’s error type. The methods are not const fn — call sites use the standard ? operator, not const-context evaluation.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::DateTime;

fn epoch_seconds(seconds: i64) -> Result<DateTime, jiff::Error> {
    DateTime::from_second(seconds)
}

let now = DateTime::now();
let later = epoch_seconds(1_700_000_000)?;
let _ = (now, later);
Ok::<(), jiff::Error>(())
}

Date — calendar date

Date represents a time-zone-free calendar date. Wire format: RFC 3339 calendar date text ("YYYY-MM-DD").

ConstructorReturnsNotes
Date::new(year: i16, month: i8, day: i8)Dateconst fn; out-of-range triple is a const-eval error

Date::new is const fn — an out-of-range (year, month, day) triple is rejected at cargo build time, not at runtime:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::Date;

const RELEASED: Date = Date::new(2027, 1, 1);
// const INVALID: Date = Date::new(2027, 13, 1); // would not compile
}

date! macro — hyphen-literal calendar dates

ferra::date!(YYYY-MM-DD) re-tokenises a hyphen-literal into Date::new(year, month, day). Same compile-time validation as Date::new:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::{Date, date};

const SUNSET: Date = date!(2027-01-01);
// const INVALID: Date = date!(2027-13-01); // const-eval error
}

The macro is the recommended call site for fixed dates (release sunsets, scheduled migrations) because the literal form is most readable. Use Date::new(...) directly when the inputs are computed or come from configuration.

Time — time of day

Time is a time of day without date or time zone. Wire format: "HH:MM:SS", with an optional fraction ("09:30:00", "23:59:59.5").

ConstructorReturnsNotes
Time::new(hour: i8, minute: i8, second: i8)Timeconst fn; an out-of-range triple is a const-eval error
"09:30:00".parse::<Time>()Result<Time, jiff::Error>FromStr

DateTime and Date implement FromStr too (RFC 3339 text).

Use as model fields

The three types are column types. Each maps to one Postgres type and round-trips through the database and through JSON:

Field typePostgres columnJSON
ferra::DateTimetimestamptz"2026-10-01T09:30:00Z" (RFC 3339, UTC)
ferra::Datedate"2026-10-01"
ferra::Timetime"09:30:00"

Option<T> of each is a nullable column. Postgres stores microseconds: a DateTime or a Time is rounded down to the microsecond when written, so what you read back is the written value truncated to microseconds.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::{Date, DateTime, FerraModel, Time};
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "events")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub at: DateTime,          // timestamptz NOT NULL
    pub day: Date,             // date NOT NULL
    pub opens: Time,           // time NOT NULL
    pub ends_at: Option<DateTime>, // timestamptz NULL
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

Import the three from ferra, not from Sea-ORM’s prelude, which has types of the same names: an explicit use ferra::{Date, DateTime, Time}; takes precedence over the glob (and use ferra::prelude::* does the same for an application that declares no sea-orm). There is no timetz, no zone-less date-time and no duration type yet.

These types are columns because ferra-core implements Sea-ORM’s value traits for them, behind its sea-orm Cargo feature. Do not enable that feature yourself: ferra-db enables it, so it is on in every application that uses the ferra facade. It is tied to Sea-ORM 2.x and adds no I/O dependency to ferra-core.

Use as deprecation dates

FoundryBuilder::deprecated(since, sunset) takes two Dates and returns Result<_, DeprecationError>: a sunset earlier than since is refused. Every response under the deprecated version carries Deprecation: @<seconds> (RFC 9745: the start of since, UTC) and Sunset: <HTTP-date> (RFC 8594: the last second of sunset, for example Tue, 05 Jan 2027 23:59:59 GMT):

use ferra::{Foundry, date};
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let app = Foundry::new(conn)
    .api_version("v1")?
    .mount::<Film>()
    .deprecated(date!(2026-07-01), date!(2027-01-05))?
    .build();
let _ = app;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

Banned imports

A field typed with another time library does not compile: #[derive(FerraModel)] rejects a field whose type path starts with chrono::, time:: or jiff::, and names the Ferra type to use instead:

error: field type uses the `chrono` time crate; a Ferra model types time values with `ferra::DateTime` (an instant), `ferra::Date` (a calendar date) or `ferra::Time` (a time of day)
         help: replace it with `ferra::DateTime`, `ferra::Date` or `ferra::Time` (Postgres `timestamptz`, `date`, `time`); the wire format is RFC 3339
         note: docs/user-guide/ferra-core.md § Time vocabulary

cargo deny check also bans the chrono and time crates from the dependency graph, except where the Sea-ORM ecosystem and Ferra’s own column adapter use them.

Why newtypes

The three newtypes are #[repr(transparent)] over the underlying library’s value types. The layout is identical to the inner type, so a future release that replaces the underlying library does so at the ferra-core::time module boundary alone — consumer-facing signatures stay stable. The inner field is pub(crate); consumers reach the value only through ferra::DateTime / ferra::Date.

The OpenAPI schema emission is encapsulated in the same module: DateTime and Date emit {type: "string", format: "date-time"} and {type: "string", format: "date"}; Time emits {type: "string", pattern: "^([01][0-9]|2[0-3]):[0-5][0-9]:[0-5][0-9](\.[0-9]{1,9})?$"} (JSON Schema’s time format requires a time-zone offset, which a time of day does not have). Consumers and downstream crates never write the schema literal — the typed-newtype contract preserves the framework’s “single source of truth” rule.

Public surface

RequestContext

RequestContext (canonical path: ferra::request_context::RequestContext) is the request-scoped handle the framework hands to application code: the ctx parameter of FerraComputed::compute_async and FerraComputed::compute_async_batch (empty there in 0.13), and the context of the authorities and hooks that read it. It answers who the caller is and what the request carried:

AccessorAnswers
subject() -> Option<&str>the caller’s FerraIdentity::id(), None when anonymous
is_authenticated() -> boola verified identity is present
has_role(&str) -> boolthe identity’s FerraIdentity::has_role
claims::<C>() -> Option<&C>the typed claims of a bearer or cookie token; None for an API key, an anonymous request, or when C is not the type given to .with_auth::<C>()
api_key() -> Option<&ApiKeyIdentity>the identity of the API key that authenticated the request
header(&str) -> Option<&str>the first value of a request header, case-insensitive; None when absent or not UTF-8

A model with neither an authority nor owner(from) gets RequestContext::empty(): every accessor answers None or false.

A hook receives the context of the model it is declared on, and tx.resource::<N>() hands that same context to the authority of N (not a context built for N).

  • Credentials never reach it. Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, Cookie and the Foundry’s API key header are dropped when the context is built, in any case, so header() answers None for them, and Clone and Debug cannot carry them. Debug prints the subject and the header names, never a value.
  • Every other header is client-supplied. header("X-Forwarded-For") returns what the client sent, as is: do not authorize on X-Forwarded-*, Forwarded, Host or Origin unless your own trusted proxy sets them.
  • Not Copy. Since 0.13.0 the type owns an Arc and a header list: it is Clone, no longer Copy, UnwindSafe or RefUnwindSafe (migration note).

For the consumer-facing usage of the surrounding pipeline, see ferra-forge.md § Computed fields.

JSON documents

serde_json::Value, bare Value, Sea-ORM’s prelude alias Json, and their Option forms are JSON fields. A typed Serialize + Deserialize struct stored with Sea-ORM’s FromJsonQueryResult opts in with #[field(json)]. sea_orm::Value is a SQL value enum and is not a JSON document type.

Before typed deserialization, a JSON field allows at most 32 container levels and 65,536 compact serialized bytes. Overrides use #[field(json(max_depth = 8, max_bytes = 4096))]; max_depth accepts 1–126, max_bytes a positive integer. Exceeding a limit returns 422 json_too_deep or json_too_large before any write. The JSON parser’s own 128-level limit returns 400 invalid_json first. An optional field accepts null. JSON fields cannot be filtered, sorted, or cursor keys (FRG-355).

An application declaring Sea-ORM with default-features = false must enable "with-json" beside "macros", "runtime-tokio-rustls", and "sqlx-postgres". ferra::meta::FieldMeta::json exposes the compiled JsonBounds description.

ferra-db — the database layer

The repository layer (PgRepository, FerraRepository, FerraDbError) is internal to Ferra and outside the contract: the ferra facade does not export it, and an application does not declare ferra-db. What an application reaches from this layer is Page, CursorPage, CollectionQuery, CursorQuery, PkValue and DatabaseConnection, all exported by ferra.

To read and write a model from a route of your own, take a Resource<M> extractor (from the ResourceHandle<M> that mount_and_handle::<M>() returns): get, list, list_cursor, create, update, delete, each returning FerraError (Custom Handlers). Behaviour that used to be read on the repository (SQLSTATE 23505 becomes a 409 Conflict, a missing row a 404, an undecodable cursor a 400) is read on the HTTP side and on FerraError (ferra-http.md). For raw access, use your own DatabaseConnection, outside the contract: see Custom Handlers § Raw database access, outside the contract. Transactions are the same: begin one on your own connection with conn.begin() (below).

Dependencies. The examples on this page assume the dependencies of Getting started:

[dependencies]
ferra   = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.13.1" }
sea-orm = { version = "2.0", default-features = false, features = ["macros", "runtime-tokio-rustls", "sqlx-postgres"] }
tokio   = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread"] }
axum    = "0.8"
serde   = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }

Queries and pages

CollectionQuery and CursorQuery are #[non_exhaustive]: build one with CollectionQuery::new(page, per_page) and the with_filter / with_sort methods, CursorQuery::new(per_page) and with_after / with_filter. A filter key the model does not declare #[field(filterable)] is refused, never ignored (Pagination). PkValue<M> is the Sea-ORM primary-key value type of M: a plain i32 / i64 / Uuid, or a tuple for a composite key (ferra-forge.md § Composite primary keys).

A filter key is the field name for equality, or field[op] for a comparison (gt, gte, lt, lte) on a ferra::DateTime, Date or Time field, as filter[field][op] is on the wire; a comparison on another type is refused (400 unsupported_operator). A CursorQuery walks ascending unless with_direction(SortDirection::Desc) says otherwise; a cursor issued for the other direction is refused as an invalid cursor, and Resource::list_cursor applies the same checks as the generated route.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::{CursorQuery, SortDirection};

let newest_first = CursorQuery::new(20)
    .with_direction(SortDirection::Desc)
    .with_filter("created_at[gte]", "2026-10-03T00:00:00Z");
assert_eq!(newest_first.direction, SortDirection::Desc);
}

Logging and tracing of database activity

sea_orm::Database::connect(&database_url) — the connection form used throughout this guide — accepts anything that converts Into<ConnectOptions>, including a bare &str. When you pass a bare URL, Sea-ORM builds a ConnectOptions with its own defaults, and those defaults are logging-on:

SettingDefaultWhat it emits
sqlx_loggingtrueEvery executed SQL statement is logged via the log/tracing bridge, at the level below.
sqlx_logging_levellog::LevelFilter::InfoThe level statements above are logged at (ignored if sqlx_logging is false).
record_stmt_in_spanstrueThe rendered SQL statement — including its bound parameter values — is attached to the tracing span for that query.
sqlx_slow_statements_logging_settings(LevelFilter::Off, _)Off by default; when enabled, statements slower than a threshold you set log at a separate level.

The bound-parameter detail on record_stmt_in_spans is the one to read twice: if a query binds a user’s email address, a password-reset token, or any other sensitive field value, that value reaches whatever sink your tracing-subscriber Layer forwards spans to — by default, with no opt-in step. This is a real disclosure surface, not a hypothetical one; treat it exactly like any other case where sensitive data could reach a log line.

A reader of this section alone can now answer: does query text reach my logs and traces by default, and how do I change that? Yes, by default, on both counts (statement logging and span recording independently). To change it, build a ConnectOptions explicitly instead of passing a bare URL string, and connect with that:

use ferra::sea_orm::{ConnectOptions, Database};

async fn demo(database_url: String) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let mut opt = ConnectOptions::new(database_url);
opt.sqlx_logging(false)           // stop logging statements entirely, or...
   .record_stmt_in_spans(false);  // ...keep statement-shape logging but never
                                   // attach the rendered SQL (with bound values)
                                   // to a span.

let conn = Database::connect(opt).await?;
let _ = conn;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

ConnectOptions’s setters take &mut self and return &mut Self, so they chain on an existing let mut binding as shown — they are not a consuming builder, and ConnectOptions::new(url) must be bound to a variable before you call a setter on it.

Recommended production posture. Disable sqlx_logging (or drop the level to a value your production log pipeline filters out) and disable record_stmt_in_spans for any connection that will ever execute a query with sensitive bound parameters — which, in a typical Ferra API, is most of them. Keep both enabled in local development, where seeing the generated SQL is a debugging aid and the log sink is your own terminal. There is no framework-level override that does this for you today — ferra-db accepts whatever sea_orm::DatabaseConnection you construct and does not itself configure ConnectOptions — so the setting is entirely in your hands at the Database::connect(...) call site.

The Page<M> shape

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::Page;
use ferra::model::FerraModel;

// The four public fields of `Page<M>`; `CursorPage<M>` has `items`, `per_page` and `next_cursor`.
fn summary<M: FerraModel>(page: &Page<M>) -> String {
    format!(
        "page {} of {} per page: {} items, {} in all",
        page.page,
        page.per_page,
        page.items.len(),
        page.total
    )
}
}
  • 1-indexed page by framework convention. page = 0 is treated identically to page = 1 (the repository applies saturating_sub(1) internally to hand Sea-ORM its 0-indexed offset).
  • total: u64 fits any Postgres bigint in the non-negative half — the full-table row count observed by the count query.
  • items.len() <= per_page always. An over-scrolled request is Ok(Page { items: vec![], total, .. }), never NotFound.
  • Concurrent-insert drift. items.len() and total may disagree by ±1 under concurrent inserts — both queries run serially on the same connection (FR-015), not in parallel. Callers that need strict consistency read inside a SERIALIZABLE transaction of their own connection.
  • Serialize, not Deserialize. Page<T>: serde::Serialize whenever T: serde::Serialize. Page<T> and CursorPage<T> accept any T, a model or a view of one, which is what lets a route of your own return a page of views (Page<M> and CursorPage<M> are the same types with T = M). No Deserialize — pages are server-constructed, never parsed from client input.
  • #[non_exhaustive] — a later release may add fields. Construct via Page::new(items, total, page, per_page), not a struct literal.

Transactions

Transactions are Sea-ORM’s: begin one on your own DatabaseConnection (the type of your own sea-orm declaration, also exported as ferra::DatabaseConnection). It needs Sea-ORM’s TransactionTrait in scope. Dropping the transaction without .commit() rolls it back. A Resource<M> call runs on its own connection, not inside your transaction; inside it, write with Sea-ORM.

use ferra::DatabaseConnection;
use sea_orm::TransactionTrait; // import needed for .begin()

async fn demo(conn: DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let tx = conn.begin().await?;
// ... Sea-ORM statements on `&tx` ...
tx.commit().await?; // dropped without commit: rolled back
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

Blameable models and the repository

The public FerraRepository write methods (insert, update, soft_delete, restore and their _in_tx forms) take no subject, so on a #[behavior(blameable)] model they return an error and write nothing: the author comes from the caller’s identity, which only the generated routes and Resource<M> hold (0.13.0).

No raw-SQL entry point

The root of the ferra crate publishes NO entry point that accepts a pre-formed SQL string: ferra::Statement, ferra::execute_unprepared and ferra::raw_sql do not resolve (compile-fail fixtures, crates/ferra/tests/ui/no_raw_sql.rs). That is not a limit on your application — ferra::sea_orm is Sea-ORM itself, and your application owns its DatabaseConnection. It is a statement about the routes Ferra generates: they never put request data in SQL text. A filter value is bound as a parameter, a sort key that is not declared #[field(sortable)] is not an identifier of the query, a cursor is decoded before any query is built (crates/ferra-db/tests/hostile_input_is_bound.rs).

Your own SQL

If you need raw SQL (a hand-written migration, an analytics query that defeats Sea-ORM’s builder), use Sea-ORM directly, on the connection you already hold. It is outside the guarantee above — the query is yours:

[dependencies]
ferra   = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.13.1" }
sea-orm = { version = "2.0", default-features = false, features = ["macros", "runtime-tokio-rustls", "sqlx-postgres"] }

One rule goes with that line: a Ferra project never holds two major versions of Sea-ORM, not even for its tests or an optional feature. A sea-orm = "1" in [dev-dependencies], or behind a feature such as full = ["dep:sea-orm"], next to a model written through the facade, is refused with FRG-400 as soon as the test or the feature is on. Give it the same major as Ferra, or remove it and write ferra::sea_orm::...; cargo tree -d -i sea-orm lists the copies (docs/user-guide/ferra-forge-diagnostics.md section FRG-400).

Your code reads as “I am opting out of Ferra’s SQL-injection-by-construction contract for this query”. Three entry points, in order of preference:

  • sea_orm::raw_sql! (added in Sea-ORM 2.0) — a format!-style macro that still parameterizes every interpolated value, so it carries no injection risk despite the format!-like syntax. This is Sea-ORM’s own recommended entry point for hand-written SQL as of 2.0. SomeEntity::find_by_statement(raw_sql!(DbBackend::Postgres, "SELECT * FROM films WHERE year > {}", min_year)).
  • Statement::from_sql_and_values — construct a Statement with an explicit parameter list (Vec<Value>) bound positionally ($1, $2, …). Use when you need to build the parameter list programmatically rather than at a single macro call site.
  • execute_unprepared (a ConnectionTrait method, e.g. conn.execute_unprepared("...").await?) — runs a literal SQL string with no parameter binding at all. Only ever pass a compile-time-constant string (a migration statement, a DDL command); passing anything containing interpolated request data here reintroduces the exact injection risk Ferra’s core contract exists to foreclose. Statement::from_string (construct-only, no execution) exists for cases where you need a Statement value without binding parameters — pair it with from_sql_and_values rather than execute_unprepared if the statement takes any input.

API keys

ferra::api_key holds the key store contract (ApiKeyStore, PgApiKeyStore), issue, revoke and the schema. How a key is issued, stored hashed and presented is in ferra-auth.md, section API keys.

The ferra facade

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::{
    Page, CursorPage, CollectionQuery, CursorQuery, PkValue,
    DatabaseConnection, Id, FerraModel, Resource, ResourceHandle,
};
}

#[derive(FerraModel)] is exported too (and by ferra::prelude): there is no second dependency to declare. The description of a model (ModelMeta, FieldMeta, FieldType) is read through the ferra::meta module.

Entity declaration: two forms

The split form — a Model struct plus a separate enum Relation { ... } naming every relation. Sea-ORM 2.0 also ships a second, terser dense form, and both are valid ways to declare a Ferra entity. This section states which to write and when, rather than leaving you to infer it from the fact that Ferra’s own shipped examples use both.

The split form

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub title: String,
}

#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}   // names every relation, even when there are none

impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

The dense form (Sea-ORM 2.0)

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[sea_orm::model]      // <- layered above the same derive list
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub title: String,
    // relations, if any, are declared inline on the struct — see below —
    // there is no separate `enum Relation` at all in this form.
}

impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

The dense form drops the enum Relation { ... } boilerplate entirely — for a model with no relations, that is a pure line-count win. When a model does have relations, the dense form declares them inline instead of in the separate enum, and FerraModel reads such a model since 0.13.0 (see ferra-forge.md § Relations for a compiled example):

// Sea-ORM's own syntax, shown for the shape.
#[sea_orm::model]
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "users")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    #[sea_orm(has_one)]
    pub profile: HasOne<super::profile::Entity>,
    #[sea_orm(has_many)]
    pub posts: HasMany<super::post::Entity>,
}

Relation fields and FerraModel

Before 0.13.0 #[derive(FerraModel)] refused HasOne<...>, HasMany<...> and BelongsTo<...> as field types, so a dense-form model with a relation field had to be written in the split form. It no longer is: #[sea_orm::model] keeps the relation fields off Model (they live on a second struct, ModelEx), Ferra reads Model, and a relation field is never a column, a wire field or a projection field. The practical rule:

Your model has…Write it as…
No relation fieldsEither form. The dense form (#[sea_orm::model]) is shorter — prefer it for new models.
One or more relation fields (has_one / has_many / belongs_to)The dense form. A split-form model gets no relation feature: a model that gains relations moves to the dense form (ADR-0059).

Which shipped example uses which, and why

  • examples/hello-ferra — its one model, Film, has no relations. It uses the dense form.
  • examples/movie-stars — its five models (Film, Actor, Director, Studio, Genre) have no relations: each declares an empty enum Relation {}. It keeps the split form by the author’s decision (ADR-0050), not because Ferra requires it. The earlier reason, that the split form scales to the relations the example would grow, no longer holds (ADR-0059): a split-form model gets no relation feature, so a model that gains relations moves to the dense form. If you have a model with no relations, the dense form is still the one to prefer.

The two shipped examples therefore show both forms; the guide states which one each uses, and hello-ferra is the reference for a new model.

Troubleshooting

error[E0277]: the trait bound <M>: sea_orm::ModelTrait is not satisfied

You forgot the DeriveEntityModel derive on the struct. A Ferra model requires BOTH FerraModel AND DeriveEntityModel on the same #[derive(...)] list. Add DeriveEntityModel back and recompile.

error[E0425]: cannot find value Statement in crate ferra

Expected — the root of ferra has no raw-SQL entry point. Use Sea-ORM’s own (sea_orm::Statement), through the sea-orm your application declares; see “Your own SQL”.

ferra::PgRepository, ferra::FerraRepository, ferra::FerraDbError, ferra::DatabaseTransaction do not resolve

Removed from the facade in 0.10.0 (the repository layer is internal). Use Resource<M> or your own DatabaseConnection (see the top of this page).

Stability commitment

What is guaranteed is what ferra exports and api/ferra.txt snapshots; a change of it needs a minor version bump (stability.md).

ItemCommitmentChange requires
CollectionQuery, CursorQuery, Page, CursorPage#[non_exhaustive], built with new and the with_* methodsAdditions are additive
DatabaseConnection re-exportStable name, re-exported from Sea-ORMA minor version
No raw-SQL entry point at the root of ferraStatement / execute_unprepared / raw_sql do not resolve there; ferra::sea_orm is Sea-ORM wholeA minor version

MSRV: rust-version = "1.94" — inherited from the workspace, and set by Sea-ORM itself.

ferra-http — the Axum CRUD handler layer

The HTTP layer: what Foundry mounts for a model, the wire contracts of the routes (RFC 7807 errors, flat and HAL representations, pagination, Prefer:), and the default layer stack. An application reaches it through the ferra facade and does not declare ferra-http; what is public is the list of stability.md, and the signatures are the snapshot api/ferra-http.txt. The response envelopes (ItemResponse, CollectionResponse), the link builders and PaginationParams are not public in 0.9: a route of your own answers with a struct of its own (Custom Handlers).

This page is the authoritative user-guide for ferra-http. A reader with only this page plus standard Rust knowledge produces a compiling Foundry::new(conn).mount::<Film>().build() call site on the first attempt — no ADR, no constitution, and no framework source is required.

Dependencies and URLs

The examples on this page assume the dependencies of Getting started:

[dependencies]
ferra   = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.13.1" }
sea-orm = { version = "2.0", default-features = false, features = ["macros", "runtime-tokio-rustls", "sqlx-postgres"] }
tokio   = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread"] }
axum    = "0.8"
serde   = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }

A model’s URL segment ({resource} below) is its table name: table_name = "films" is served at /films. To serve a table under another name, put #[ferra(resource = "movies")] on the model. A model’s table is its own to create (a migration, or Schema::create_table_from_entity in development): Ferra never creates one.

Zero-to-API in five lines

use ferra::Foundry;
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
async fn demo(database_url: String) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let conn = sea_orm::Database::connect(&database_url).await?;
let app = Foundry::new(conn).mount::<Film>().build();
let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:3000").await?;
axum::serve(listener, app.into_make_service_with_connect_info::<std::net::SocketAddr>()).await?;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

Film here is declared #[ferra(auth = "none")]. A model that needs an identity (auth = "bearer", or #[authorize] rules other than Anyone) must be mounted on a chain with .with_auth::<YourClaims>(jwt) — see ferra-auth.md. Foundry is the only way to mount a model: it is what applies the model’s authorization rules. There is no lower-level router constructor.

You get GET /films, GET /films/{id}, POST /films, PUT /films/{id} and DELETE /films/{id}, a Location header on creation, and an application/problem+json body on every error. The primary key may be single or composite. Serve with into_make_service_with_connect_info: the rate limiter keys on the peer address.

See examples/hello-ferra/ for the full worked example with PostgreSQL container + Rust-coded migrations.

The routes a model gets

Foundry mounts these routes for every model; the handlers behind them are internal. The HTTP contracts are:

OperationMethodPathRequestSuccessError surfaces
getGET/{resource}/{id}—200 OK + the row as JSON (HAL: with _links)400 on path-extractor rejection · 404 on missing row · 500 on DB error
listGET/{resource}?page={u32}&per_page={u32}200 OK + the collection as JSON (HAL: with _links)500 on DB error
createPOST/{resource}JSON body of the write projection201 Created + Location: {base}/{resource}/{id} + the row as JSON (HAL: with _links); 201 with no body and no Location when the caller may not GET the new row400 on body parse · 401/403 from the rule · 409 on unique violation · 413 on oversized body · 422 on a field outside the write projection or a #[field(...)] rule · 429 on rate limit · 500
updatePUT/{resource}/{id}JSON body of the write projection200 OK + the row as JSON (HAL: with _links); 204 with no body when the caller may not GET the updated row (0.13.0)400 · 401/403 · 404 · 409 · 413 · 422 · 429 · 500
deleteDELETE/{resource}/{id}—204 No Content (no body)400 · 404 · 429 · 500

The path names the row on update and delete; a key in the body is refused (422). The rule is checked before the body is read. See Projections and routing § Writes for what a write body may contain.

Public reads, protected writes

A model that must be readable without a token but writable only with one says so per operation, and the chain names the claims type. A field is sortable (?sort=-price_cents) or filterable (?filter[name]=…) only if it says so with #[field(sortable)] / #[field(filterable)] (Pagination). The table is shop_products and the URL is /products: #[ferra(resource = "products")] sets the URL segment; without it, the segment is the table name (/shop_products):

use ferra::{ClaimCheck, FerraIdentity, FerraModel, Foundry, HmacAlgorithm, JwtConfig};
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

mod product {
    use super::*;

    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "shop_products")]
    #[ferra(auth = "bearer", resource = "products")]
    #[authorize(
        list = Anyone,
        get = Anyone,
        create = Authenticated,
        update = Authenticated,
        delete = Authenticated
    )]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        #[field(filterable)]
        pub name: String,
        #[field(sortable)]
        pub price_cents: i64,
    }

    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}

    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

#[derive(Clone, Debug, Deserialize)]
struct Claims {
    sub: String,
}

impl FerraIdentity for Claims {
    fn id(&self) -> &str {
        &self.sub
    }
    fn has_role(&self, _role: &str) -> bool {
        false
    }
}

fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let jwt = JwtConfig::single_secret(
    "key-1",                                        // `kid`: every token must carry it
    std::env::var("JWT_SECRET")?,                   // the HMAC secret, from the environment
    HmacAlgorithm::Hs256,
    ClaimCheck::expect("https://auth.example.com/"), // `iss` the token must carry
    ClaimCheck::expect("products-api"),              // `aud` the token must carry
)?;
let app = Foundry::new(conn)
    .with_auth::<Claims>(jwt)
    .mount::<product::Model>()
    .build();
let _ = app;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

(Authentication and Authorization has the rest of the JWT configuration.)

A model that carries one or more #[ferra(projection(...))] declarations also mounts a parallel set of routes under each named projection’s URL prefix (e.g. /detail/films/{id}). The wire shape on those routes is the projection’s own: a response is serialized from its read struct, and a body is parsed into its write struct. See Projections and routing for the full URL contract, naming convention, and the path_prefix override.

RFC 7807 error taxonomy

Every error from every handler is rendered as application/problem+json per RFC 7807 §3. FerraError has fourteen variants (the enum is #[non_exhaustive], so a match outside the crate needs a wildcard arm; FerraError::error_type() names the wire type of any variant). They map onto twelve of the fourteen type URIs (the others, payload_too_large and rate_limited, come from middleware layers, see Error handling):

VariantHTTP statustype URItitle
FerraError::NotFound { resource, id }404https://ferra.rs/errors/not_foundResource Not Found
FerraError::CollectionNotFound { resource }404https://ferra.rs/errors/not_foundResource Not Found (detail <resource> not found, no id; 0.13.0)
FerraError::Validation(ValidationErrors)400https://ferra.rs/errors/validationValidation Error
FerraError::BadRequest { detail, field, code }400https://ferra.rs/errors/validationValidation Error
FerraError::Unprocessable(ValidationErrors)422https://ferra.rs/errors/validation_failedValidation Failed
FerraError::InvalidCursor400https://ferra.rs/errors/invalid_cursorInvalid Cursor
FerraError::Unauthorized401https://ferra.rs/errors/unauthorizedUnauthorized (with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer)
FerraError::Forbidden403https://ferra.rs/errors/forbiddenForbidden
FerraError::Conflict(String)409https://ferra.rs/errors/conflictConflict
FerraError::ConflictWith(String)409https://ferra.rs/errors/conflictConflict (your hook’s HookError::conflict; the detail is yours, served as given; see ferra-error-handling.md § Hook errors)
FerraError::UnsupportedMediaType415https://ferra.rs/errors/unsupported_media_typeUnsupported Media Type
FerraError::Internal(String)500https://ferra.rs/errors/internalInternal Server Error
FerraError::Timeout503https://ferra.rs/errors/timeoutRequest Timeout Budget Exceeded (no Retry-After; see foundry.md § Request time budget)
FerraError::IdentityUnavailable503https://ferra.rs/errors/identity_unavailableIdentity Unavailable (a key set out of reach with no fresh key cached; no Retry-After; see ferra-auth.md § Key set)
FerraError::ServiceUnavailable(String)503https://ferra.rs/errors/service_unavailableService Unavailable (your hook’s HookError::unavailable; the detail is yours; no Retry-After; see ferra-error-handling.md § Hook errors)
(middleware)413https://ferra.rs/errors/payload_too_largePayload Too Large 1
(middleware)429https://ferra.rs/errors/rate_limitedToo Many Requests 1

Worked body for a 404:

{
  "type":   "https://ferra.rs/errors/not_found",
  "title":  "Resource Not Found",
  "status": 404,
  "detail": "films/42 not found"
}

Worked body for a 400 from a malformed JSON request:

{
  "type":   "https://ferra.rs/errors/validation",
  "title":  "Validation Error",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "validation failed",
  "errors": [
    { "field": "body", "code": "invalid_json", "message": "expected `,` or `}` at line 1 column 14" }
  ]
}

Internals never leak. The detail field on a 500 is always the literal string "internal server error"; the inner sea_orm::DbErr is dropped before reaching the HTTP body. The Axum "Failed to deserialize … into the target type: " prefix and any axum::extract::rejection:: substring are stripped at the extractor boundary; only human-readable messages reach errors[*].message.

Worked body for a 429 from the rate-limit mapper:

{
  "type":   "https://ferra.rs/errors/rate_limited",
  "title":  "Too Many Requests",
  "status": 429,
  "detail": "rate limit exceeded; retry after 3 seconds"
}

The response also carries the Retry-After header (integer seconds, at least 1). A refill shorter than a second is answered as Retry-After: 1, never 0, which would invite an immediate retry that is refused again. If the component ever emitted no Retry-After header, detail would degrade to the literal string "rate limit exceeded" and the header would be absent from the response; the default rule always emits it. The rate-limit mapper mounts only alongside the framework’s default rate-limit component — consumer-provided rate-limiters produce their own error shape (see ADR-0015 for rationale).

Response representations

A successful response comes in two shapes, and the client chooses with Accept: flat (application/json) is the row, or the collection envelope, as plain JSON; HAL (application/hal+json) is the same body plus _links, so an AI agent can navigate the API without prior URL knowledge. Both go through the same query and the same read projection: they show the same rows, the same total and the same keys.

AcceptRepresentation
absent, empty, */*, application/*, only other types, unparseablethe Foundry default: HAL unless you set it
application/jsonflat
application/hal+jsonHAL
both, with different qthe higher q
both, with equal q (or both q=0)the Foundry default
one of the two at q=0, the other absentthe other

Ferra never answers 406: an Accept it cannot satisfy gets the default. An error is application/problem+json and the same body in both modes.

On a 2xxFlatHAL
Content-Typeapplication/jsonapplication/hal+json
VaryAcceptAccept
Location (201)yesyes

A 201 to a caller who may create the row but not GET it is the exception: no body, so no Content-Type, and no Location (0.13.0).

| Link, X-Total-Count | never | never |

Vary: Accept is on every negotiated 2xx, 204 included: configure a cache in front of the API to honor it. Pagination state is in the body only, never in a header.

To serve flat to a client that states no preference, set the default before the first mount:

use ferra::{Foundry, Representation};
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) {
let app = Foundry::new(conn)
    .default_representation(Representation::Flat)
    .mount::<Film>()
    .build();
let _ = app;
}
fn main() {}

Before 0.11.0 the HAL body was served as application/json. A client that sends Accept: application/json now gets the flat body: it no longer has _links. A client that sends no Accept still gets HAL, with the Content-Type application/hal+json.

Flat bodies

{ "id": 1, "title": "Rust en pratique", "director": "Alice", "year": 2025 }

A page list is {"items": [...], "total": 25, "page": 2, "per_page": 10}; a cursor list is {"items": [...], "per_page": 10, "next_cursor": "<token>"}, and next_cursor is null on the last page (the key is always there). Pass next_cursor back as ?cursor= with the same filter[...] and sort.

HAL single-item body

Model fields are flattened at the top level via #[serde(flatten)]. A Film { id: 1, title: "Rust en pratique", director: "Alice", year: Some(2025) } serializes as:

{
  "id": 1,
  "title": "Rust en pratique",
  "director": "Alice",
  "year": 2025,
  "_links": {
    "self":       { "href": "https://api.example.com/films/1" },
    "collection": { "href": "https://api.example.com/films" }
  }
}

HAL paginated collection body

{
  "items": [ /* array of items, each with its own _links */ ],
  "total": 25,
  "page": 2,
  "per_page": 10,
  "_links": {
    "self":  { "href": "https://api.example.com/films?page=2&per_page=10" },
    "next":  { "href": "https://api.example.com/films?page=3&per_page=10" },
    "prev":  { "href": "https://api.example.com/films?page=1&per_page=10" },
    "first": { "href": "https://api.example.com/films?page=1&per_page=10" },
    "last":  { "href": "https://api.example.com/films?page=3&per_page=10" }
  }
}

An item’s _links.self is present only if the caller may GET that row, and _links.collection only if the caller may list the collection: a caller who may list but not read a row gets the row without self, so following a link as the same caller always answers 2xx (0.13.0). Under a projection prefix every link carries it: a page served at /admin/films links to /admin/films?page=…, and its items to /admin/films/{id}. A served row has no restore link (a served row is live).

On boundary pages, next or prev serialize as JSON null (never omitted). On total == 0, last_page == 1 and first == last == self.

Every link repeats the request’s filter[...] and sort (percent-encoded), so following next stays on the same list. A cursor list in HAL also carries next_cursor, the cursor of _links.next.

Links in a route of your own

The link builders are not public in 0.9.0: they know neither the base path, the version prefix nor the configured origin that Foundry applies. A route of your own that returns a resource with links writes the _links object itself — see custom-handlers.md.

Pagination

0.7.5 Enameling — collection-read parameters widened. The new filter[<field>], sort, and cursor parameters layer on top of page / per_page without changing the existing extractor surface — see pagination.md for the consumer-facing guide (the load-bearing surface for filtering, sorting, and cursor pagination). The handler dispatches on the model’s #[ferra(pagination = …)] posture; the page-mode parameters below continue to work unchanged.

The page-mode parameters are read by the generated routes; the extractor is internal since 0.9.0. A missing page is 1 (and 0 is read as 1), a missing per_page is 20, and per_page is clamped to 1–100, silently: no Warning header (RFC 9111 §5.5 obsoletes it; the body says what applied).

  • Default: page=1, per_page=20.
  • Cap: per_page ≤ 100 (hard limit). Values below 1 or above 100 are clamped, with no Warning header (RFC 9111 §5.5 obsoletes it; before 0.12.0 the response carried Warning: 214).
  • The response body’s per_page field reports the clamped value, so a client detects a clamp by comparing it with what it asked.
  • A page or per_page that is not a non-negative integer (page=abc) is a 400 with the code invalid_parameter; it is not read as the default.

Worked curl:

$ curl -D - 'http://localhost:3000/films?per_page=500'
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
cache-control: no-store
content-type: application/hal+json
vary: Accept
vary: Authorization, Cookie
...
{"items":[...],"total":523,"page":1,"per_page":100,"_links":{...}}

Links and Location

Hypermedia links (_links, HAL-inspired) and the Location header are relative by default: /films/42, or /api/films/42 under a FerraLayer base_path. Resolve them against the URL you called, as an HTTP client does for Location. The request’s Host, X-Forwarded-Host and X-Forwarded-Proto headers are never read: a client cannot make the API emit links to another origin.

Location on a 201 is the self link of the new row (the same href a HAL read gives it), under a projection prefix as on the bare path. It is present only if self is: a caller who may create but not GET the row gets 201 Created with no body and no Location, with or without Prefer: return=minimal, so no id, stamp or author reaches a caller who may not read them (0.13.0).

To emit absolute links, configure the public origin once:

use ferra::Foundry;
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let app = Foundry::new(conn)
    .with_base_url("https://api.example.com")? // Result<_, BaseUrlError>
    .mount::<Film>()
    .build();
// Location: https://api.example.com/films/42
let _ = app;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

The value must be an http or https origin — scheme, host and optional port; a trailing / is dropped — with no path, query, fragment, userinfo (https://user:password@host) or whitespace; otherwise BaseUrlError::NotHttp, NoHost or NotAnOrigin. A path prefix is not part of the origin: declare it with FerraLayer::base_path (for instance behind a proxy that serves the API under /api).

On a versioned chain (.api_version("v1")), links carry the version prefix the routes are served under, relative or absolute: /v1/films/42, or https://api.example.com/v1/films/42 with an origin. The order is origin, then base_path, then the version prefix.

Resource<M> — a model’s rows from a route of your own

A route of your own reaches a model’s rows through Resource<M>, an axum extractor. Foundry::mount_and_handle::<M>() mounts the model and issues a ResourceHandle<M> (Foundry); the handle goes in the router state — .with_state(handle), or a field of an application state that derives axum::extract::FromRef — and the handler takes Resource<M>.

use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
use axum::{Json, Router, extract::Path, routing::get};
use ferra::model::FerraViews;
use ferra::{FerraError, Foundry, Resource};

async fn one(films: Resource<Film>, Path(id): Path<i32>)
    -> Result<Json<<Film as FerraViews>::Read>, FerraError>
{
    Ok(Json(films.get(id).await?))
}

fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) {
let (foundry, films) = Foundry::new(conn).mount_and_handle::<Film>();
let app: Router = foundry
    .build()
    .merge(Router::new().route("/films/{id}/mine", get(one)).with_state(films));
let _ = app;
}
fn main() {}
MethodDoes whatTakesReturns
getGET /{resource}/{id}the key<M as FerraViews>::Read
listGET /{resource}, page modea CollectionQueryPage<Read>
list_cursorGET /{resource}, cursor modea CursorQueryCursorPage<Read>
createPOST /{resource}<M as FerraViews>::WriteRead
updatePUT /{resource}/{id} for the fields it setsthe key, <M as FerraViews>::PatchRead
deleteDELETE /{resource}/{id}, soft on a soft-delete modelthe key()

All of them answer with a FerraError, so the refusals are those of the generated routes.

Who the caller is, and the order of refusals

The caller is bound when Resource<M> is extracted: the identity the JWT layer verified, if the request went through it; else the bearer token of the Authorization header, verified with the chain’s own JWT configuration; else nobody.

  1. A token that is present and invalid — an Authorization header that is not a well-formed Bearer credential included — is refused at extraction with the 401 the JWT layer gives, before any database statement.
  2. On a chain without .with_auth() no token is read, and the caller is anonymous: a rule that needs an identity answers 401.
  3. Your route’s own extractors (FerraPath, FerraJson) run before you call a method, so a malformed path or body can be answered 400 before the access answers 401 or 403. What the access then refuses — 401, 403, 404, 422 — is what the generated route refuses, because it is the same code: another caller’s row under IsOwner is a 404, indistinguishable from a missing row.

What it hands back

get, list and create return the model’s read view, <M as FerraViews>::Read: the {Model}ReadProjection struct #[derive(FerraModel)] generates (or the projection promoted with default = true). A #[ferra(write_only)] or #[ferra(skip)] field is not a member of that type, so a route that serializes it cannot leak it. update takes <M as FerraViews>::Patch, the generated {Model}Patch: one Option<T> per field of the write projection, None meaning “leave the column” (and Option<Option<T>> for a nullable column, Some(None) writing null). Only the set columns reach the UPDATE; a write-only column is writable and never read back.

create and update return the row they wrote with the field read rules applied, but without the can(Get) check of the model’s #[ferra(authority)] that the generated routes make before they send a body (a caller who may write a row but not read it gets no body from the route). A handler of yours must not echo that value to a caller who may not read the row: check with get first, or send nothing. The same holds for the rows tx.resource::<N>() returns inside a hook.

Limits, by design:

  • The access serves the bare route’s projections. Selecting a named projection comes with per-projection authorization, later.
  • restore is not offered.
  • The read view carries the model’s Rust field names; #[ferra(rename_all = "camelCase")] is applied by the generated routes when they serialize, not by the struct. A route of your own answers with a struct of its own.
  • A filter you put in a CollectionQuery or a CursorQuery is held to the route’s safelist: only #[field(filterable)] fields, by their Rust names, with a value of the field’s type. Under IsOwner the list holds the caller’s rows whatever filter you pass.

A handler that extracts Resource<M> from a state that carries no handle for M does not compile; see FRG-152 in the diagnostics.

Custom extractors

See custom-handlers.md — the rationale for FerraJson<T> / FerraPath<T> (RFC 7807 error continuity), the FromRequest vs FromRequestParts ordering rule, the Send + Sync + 'static cheat-sheet, and a worked end-to-end POST /films/{id}/publish action route.

Security defaults

Every route Foundry mounts carries a deny-by-default Tower layer stack:

LayerDefaultOverride path
tower_http::cors::CorsLayer::new()Deny all cross-origin; with JwtConfig::with_cookie, the listed origins only, with credentials (see CORS with the cookie)FerraLayer::cors(...), refused with the cookie
413 body-limit mapperRewrites stock text/plain → application/problem+json with type: .../payload_too_large— (permanent)
tower_http::limit::RequestBodyLimitLayer1 MiBFerraLayer::body_limit(...)
tower_http::trace::TraceLayerOne INFO event per request: method, path (no query string), status, latency in ms, and for an accepted request the kind of credential (credential = token, cookie or api_key) and a key’s api_key.prefix. Never headers, bodies, a token or a key secret.FerraLayer::trace_layer
tower_governor::GovernorLayer on mutation endpoints2 mutations per second, burst 5 (RateLimitRule::new(2, 5)) + peer-socket-IP keyFerraLayer::rate_limit(RateLimitRule::new(per_second, burst))
Cache default (outermost layer of build())Cache-Control: no-store when the response has none; Vary merged with Accept, Authorization, Cookiea route’s own Cache-Control, see Caching
per_page clamp (FR-017)Clamped to [1, 100]; the body’s per_page is the applied value (no Warning header since 0.12.0)— (constitutional)

429 wire format — the framework’s default rate-limit component’s 429 responses are rewritten to application/problem+json with type: https://ferra.rs/errors/rate_limited, with a Retry-After of at least 1 second. See the worked body in §“RFC 7807 error taxonomy” above. Oversized bodies produce the same application/problem+json shape — a client parsing type never sees a mixed wire format.

FerraLayer::new().no_rate_limit().build() removes mutation throttling and its mapper; no ConnectInfo is needed. Otherwise the default peer-IP key requires into_make_service_with_connect_info::<std::net::SocketAddr>(); a missing peer answers 500. Foundry::rate_limit_key selects trusted-proxy or custom keying before mounting (see foundry.md § Rate-limit override). On Lambda quotas are per execution environment: use no_rate_limit with API Gateway throttling (the example uses burst 20, rate 10 requests/second).

Rate-limit observability event. Each time the rate-limit mapper rewrites a 429, it emits a single structured tracing::warn! event so an operator tailing logs can see rate-limit rejections without reading the framework source:

  • Target: ferra_http::rate_limit — namespaced so an operator can isolate it via EnvFilter (RUST_LOG=ferra_http::rate_limit=warn).
  • Message: rate limit exceeded.
  • Severity: WARN.
  • Fields (deliberately minimal):
    • http.method — the request HTTP method (e.g. "POST"). Always present.
    • http.target — the request path, never the query string (e.g. "/films" for POST /films?page=2; ADR-0076). Always present.
    • http.retry_after_seconds — integer seconds parsed from the inbound Retry-After header. Present only when the header parses as a non-negative integer; genuinely absent otherwise (not recorded as 0).

Request and response body content never appear in this event — only the three fields listed above. The schema is pinned minimal so the framework’s dedicated observability phase at 0.12.0 Sheen can absorb it into span-based telemetry (adding trace_id, span_id, and peer-IP once the trusted-proxy story lands) without breaking a consumer’s existing EnvFilter or custom tracing::Layer.

Wire up a subscriber in your host binary’s main to surface these events:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
tracing_subscriber::fmt()
    .with_env_filter("ferra_http::rate_limit=warn")
    .init();
}

Layer placement (FR-006). The rate-limit mapper mounts as the outer layer of the mutation sub-router only, wrapping tower_governor::GovernorLayer from the outside (the last .layer() call on that sub-router). Consumer-added middleware appended to Foundry::…build() wraps the mapper from further outside — see §“Layer ordering — how .layer() composes” below for the full diagram.

Overriding the defaults. Every default in the table above is overridable via the FerraLayer builder applied to a Foundry chain — body cap, CORS, mutation rate-limit rule, tracing layer, and a base_path prefix on hypermedia links. The override surface is documented in foundry.md § “Transport-layer overrides” with the full worked example and the REPLACE-not-merge rule for per-model overrides.

CORS with the cookie

When the JwtConfig has with_cookie(name, origins) (ferra-auth.md § Cookie), each model’s CORS layer is built from that origin list instead of the deny-all default: a listed origin gets its exact Access-Control-Allow-Origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, any other origin gets no Access-Control-Allow-* header, and a preflight needs no credential. The same list is the CSRF guard of a write the cookie authenticates. CORS wraps the authentication layer, so what that layer answers (the 401 of an expired cookie, the 400 of two credentials, the 403 of the CSRF guard) carries the CORS headers too: a listed app can read it and tell that its session expired.

Do not set FerraLayer::cors(...) with the cookie. build() panics: “a custom CORS layer cannot be combined with the cookie credential: remove FerraLayer::cors; the origins given to JwtConfig::with_cookie drive CORS”. Two policies would leave one silently ignored, and a custom layer with allow_credentials(true) answers every origin. A chain without the cookie keeps FerraLayer::cors as it was.

Layer ordering — how .layer() composes

Tower’s .layer() wraps the current router as the inner service, so the last .layer() call becomes the outermost layer. A .layer(MyCustomLayer::new()) appended to Foundry::…build() therefore wraps every Ferra-provided layer from the outside.

Side-by-side: the conceptual stack (top = outermost, bottom = innermost) and the literal .layer() call sequence in Foundry::…build() (top = first call, bottom = last call). Arrows map the inversion:

CONCEPTUAL stack (request top→bottom):        LITERAL call sequence (first→last in source):

 outer → cache defaults (Cache-Control, Vary)   (chain level, outside everything below)
         request budget
         CorsLayer                              .layer(DefaultBodyLimit::disable())   ← first call (innermost)
         JWT / API key authentication
         body_limit_mapper                      .layer(TraceLayer::new_for_http())
         RequestBodyLimitLayer(1 MiB)           .layer(RequestBodyLimitLayer::new(1 MiB))
         TraceLayer                             .layer(middleware::from_fn(body_limit_mapper))
         DefaultBodyLimit::disable              .layer(CorsLayer::new())              ← last call (outermost)
         (on mutation sub-router:)             
           rate_limit_mapper                    [on mutation sub-router:]
           GovernorLayer                          .layer(GovernorLayer { ... })       ← first call on mutations
 inner → handlers                                .layer(middleware::from_fn(rate_limit_mapper))  ← last (outer)

Reading it: on the generated routes the order, outermost first, is cache defaults, request budget, CORS, JWT (and API key) authentication, body limit, trace, then the rate limiter on mutations. A request enters at the cache defaults (outermost), traverses down to the handler, and the response retraces the stack back out. In the source, the call order is inverted — the first .layer() call is the innermost layer on the merged router, and the last .layer() call is the outermost.

Mutation sub-router subtlety. GovernorLayer (rate-limit) and rate_limit_mapper (the 429 RFC 7807 wrapper) mount on the mutation sub-router only — never on the merged router and never on read routes. rate_limit_mapper is the last .layer() call on that sub-router, so it wraps GovernorLayer from the outside and sees the 429s that layer produces. Placing a custom observability layer is a decision about which sub-router you wrap — consumers who want to observe only mutations attach to a sub-router; consumers who want to observe everything attach to the merged router returned by Foundry::…build().

Worked consumer example. A consumer appending two custom layers on top of the framework stack:

use ferra::Foundry;
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
use axum::{extract::Request, middleware::{from_fn, Next}, response::Response};
async fn observe(request: Request, next: Next) -> Response { next.run(request).await }
async fn shed_load(request: Request, next: Next) -> Response { next.run(request).await }
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) {
let app = Foundry::new(conn).mount::<Film>().build()
    .layer(from_fn(observe))      // outer: sees requests before the framework
    .layer(from_fn(shed_load));   // appended AFTER → now the TRUE outermost
let _ = app;
}
fn main() {}

On incoming requests: shed_load runs first, then observe, then the framework stack (CORS → body_limit_mapper → RequestBodyLimitLayer → TraceLayer → DefaultBodyLimit::disable → handlers; with the mutation-only branch adding rate_limit_mapper → GovernorLayer before mutation handlers). On the way back out, responses traverse the stack in reverse.

See also §“RFC 7807 error taxonomy” for the 429 wire body the rate_limit_mapper produces.

Caching

Every response a Foundry router gives, errors included, carries Cache-Control: no-store and a Vary that names Accept, Authorization and Cookie (and the configured API key header when API keys are configured). This covers the generated routes, your .route(...) routes, /docs, a 404 or 405 before any route, the 503 of the request budget, the 413, the 429 and a CORS preflight answer. A shared cache (CDN, API gateway, proxy) therefore stores nothing and cannot replay an authenticated answer to another caller (RFC 9111 §3.5 protects Authorization only, and a 200 or 404 is cacheable with no header at all, §4.2.2).

  • Cache-Control is inserted only when the response has none: a route that sets its own Cache-Control, whatever its directives, keeps it.
  • Vary is merged, never replaced: the names the route already sent stay, the missing ones among the three are added, case-insensitively. A Vary: * is left as it is. A route that opts into caching still carries Vary: Authorization, Cookie: the entries are keyed on them (over-keying is safe).

A public route that may be cached. Declare it with .route(...) and give its MethodRouter a layer that sets Cache-Control; the default only inserts when the header is absent, so this route alone keeps its directive:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use axum::{http::{HeaderValue, header}, response::Response, routing::get};
use ferra::Foundry;

fn configure(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) {
    let cacheable = get(|| async { "a public page" }).layer(
        axum::middleware::map_response(|mut response: Response| async move {
            response.headers_mut().insert(
                header::CACHE_CONTROL,
                HeaderValue::from_static("public, max-age=60"),
            );
            response
        }),
    );
    let _router = Foundry::new(conn).route("/public", cacheable).build();
}
}

tower_http::set_header::SetResponseHeaderLayer::overriding does the same; it needs the set-header feature of tower-http, which Ferra does not enable, so your application declares it. A generated model route has no such knob before 1.0.

Warning. Do not add a layer that overwrites Cache-Control to the Router that build() returns: it wraps Ferra’s default and replaces no-store on every route, authenticated ones included. Ferra cannot see it and does not refuse it. FoundryBuilder::layer takes a FerraLayer, which cannot set Cache-Control: its knobs are CORS, body limit, rate limit, trace and base path, and trace_layer takes a TraceLayer, which does not set response headers. Only a layer added to the Router after build() can override no-store.

Responses that depend on the caller

A response whose content depends on who asks carries no-store and the full Vary above. Tests prove it on each such surface: a field only some roles read, a list scoped to the caller’s own rows, a list narrowed by an authority and GET /me. No generated response carries public or s-maxage, whatever the model, the operation or the identity.

What the guarantee does not cover is yours: the responses of your .route(...) handlers, which keep any Cache-Control they set, and a layer you add after build(). A public or s-maxage there lets a shared cache replay a caller’s answer to another (OWASP API8, security misconfiguration).

Write bodies reject unknown fields

Both write paths now refuse a request body carrying a field the model does not declare, with HTTP 422 and an application/problem+json body naming every offending field.

Since 0.8.0 (a break from 0.7). Through 0.7.x the two paths disagreed: projection-routed writes were already strict, while bare-path (POST /films, PUT /films/{id}) writes silently dropped unknown fields and returned 201 / 200. The same model therefore enforced two different postures depending on which URL a consumer addressed. That divergence is closed; the bare path is now strict too.

Why strict. The model’s field set is the safelist. A typed model surface that silently discards consumer-supplied fields is the silent-tolerance shape adjacent to mass assignment — a client sends {"role": "admin"}, receives 200, and has no signal that the field went nowhere. The industry is genuinely split here (Stripe and OWASP allowlisting on one side, Postel’s-law tolerant-reader on the other); Ferra picks strict as a deliberate security-over-convenience arbitration, not as a claim of consensus.

Migrating. Request bodies must match the model’s declared field set.

  • Remove fields your model does not declare. If a client was sending them and relying on the drop, that reliance was silent and is now visible — which is the point.
  • A field you want accepted must exist on the model, or on the projection’s write = [...] set for a projection-routed write.
  • Every offending field is reported in one response; the framework does not stop at the first.
  • Since 0.9.0 the bare path reads the model’s default write projection, which leaves out the primary key, the owner, read-only, skipped and computed fields, and the behavior columns: a body carrying any of them is a 422 too (see Projections and routing § Writes).

The OpenAPI document says so. It carries additionalProperties: false on every write-body schema, so generated clients and API-discovering agents see the same strictness the server enforces.

Content negotiation — RFC 7240 Prefer: header

Every mutation endpoint (POST, PUT, DELETE) recognises the RFC 7240 Prefer: request header and branches the response shape accordingly. Consumers that do not send the header observe the default shape.

Recognised tokens

Prefer: valueEffectResulting statusResponse body
(header absent)default mutation shapePOST → 201 Created, PUT → 200 OK, DELETE → 204full resource body on POST/PUT; empty on DELETE
return=minimalomit the response bodyPOST → 204 No Content (Location preserved, for a caller who may GET the new row; one who may not gets 201 with no body and no Location), PUT → 204, DELETE → 204 unchangedempty
return=representationexplicit form of the defaultPOST → 201, PUT → 200, DELETE → 204 unchangedfull resource body
respond-asyncparse-only — recognised so clients can probe the header without being broken, but has no effect on the response shape. Reserved for a future async-jobs cohort.unchangedunchanged

A caller who may PUT or restore a row but not GET it gets 204 No Content with no body whatever it asked, as a create gets its 201 with no body (0.13.0): the write is done, nothing of the row leaves. Preference-Applied: return=minimal is echoed only when return=minimal was asked, never return=representation. A hand-written route on Resource::update serves what it chooses.

The parser is case-insensitive, whitespace-tolerant, and silently drops unrecognised tokens and ;-delimited parameters per RFC 7240 §2 (“recipients SHOULD ignore preferences they do not understand”):

Prefer: Return=Minimal, respond-async; wait=10

…parses as return=minimal + respond-async (the ; wait=10 parameter is dropped).

Preference-Applied: response header

Per RFC 7240 §3, the framework echoes honoured preferences via the Preference-Applied: response header. The header is absent when no preference was honoured — including the no-header case (table row 1) and the unrecognised-token case.

Request Prefer:Response Preference-Applied:
(absent)absent
return=minimalreturn=minimal (also for a caller who may not GET the row: it gets no body whatever it asked, and the echo says only what it asked)
return=representationreturn=representation (echoed even though the body is unchanged — the standard binds the echo to “preferences that were honoured”, not to “preferences that changed the response”), except for a caller who may not GET the row it just created, updated or restored: it gets no body, so return=representation is not honoured and not echoed (0.13.0)
respond-asyncabsent (parse-only — no observable change)
return=minimal, respond-asyncreturn=minimal (only the honoured preference is echoed)
handling=lenient (unrecognised)absent

Interaction with the 422 validation path

When a mutation request fails declarative validation (the application/problem+json 422 path), the Prefer: header is recognised but does not change the response. The 422 body is mandated by the framework’s closed-namespace contract; Preference-Applied: is not emitted on the 422 path (no preference was honoured that changed observable behaviour).

Worked example

# Default — full body returned.
curl -i -X POST https://api.example.com/films \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title": "Inception", "director": "Christopher Nolan", "year": 2010}'

# HTTP/1.1 201 Created
# Content-Type: application/json
# Location: /films/42
# { "id": 42, "title": "Inception", ... }

# `return=minimal` — body omitted, Location preserved.
curl -i -X POST https://api.example.com/films \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Prefer: return=minimal' \
  -d '{"title": "Inception", "director": "Christopher Nolan", "year": 2010}'

# HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
# Location: /films/43
# Preference-Applied: return=minimal

Batch-processing consumers gain bandwidth and JSON-parse savings on every mutation.

The ferra facade

[dependencies] ferra = { git = "…", tag = "…" } is the entry point (the facade package is ferra; nothing is published on crates.io). Resource, FerraError, FerraJson, FerraPath and Foundry are named from this single dependency, alongside the #[derive(FerraModel)] macro (use ferra::{FerraModel, Foundry};; use ferra::prelude::*; opens them all, for an application that declares no sea-orm of its own). The exact list of what ferra exports is stability.md.

Consumers do not depend on ferra-core, ferra-db, ferra-forge, or ferra-http directly. A compile-fail fixture pins ferra::Statement, ferra::execute_unprepared and ferra::raw_sql as unreachable: the root of the facade has no raw-SQL entry point. ferra::sea_orm is Sea-ORM itself; what Ferra guarantees is about the routes it generates.

Worked end-to-end example

use ferra::{FerraModel, Foundry};
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

mod film {
    use super::*;

    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")] // deliberately public: this example has no JWT
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        #[sea_orm(unique)]
        pub title: String,
        pub director: String,
        pub year: Option<i32>,
    }

    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}

    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

pub use film::Model as Film;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let database_url = std::env::var("DATABASE_URL")?;
    let conn = sea_orm::Database::connect(&database_url).await?;
    let app = Foundry::new(conn).mount::<Film>().build();
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:3000").await?;
    axum::serve(listener, app.into_make_service_with_connect_info::<std::net::SocketAddr>()).await?;
    Ok(())
}

See examples/hello-ferra/ for the full three-command boot sequence (docker compose up -d postgres or podman compose up -d postgres → sea-orm-cli migrate up → cargo run -p hello-ferra) and the smoke.sh script that exercises all seven wire-format contracts.

Troubleshooting

413 vs 400 on oversized bodies

A request whose body exceeds the 1 MiB default cap is rejected either with 413 Payload Too Large or with 400 Bad Request, depending on a single precondition: whether the request declares a Content-Length header.

RequestResponse codetype URIResponsible mapper
Body > 1 MiB with Content-Length declared413https://ferra.rs/errors/payload_too_largebody_limit_mapper (FR-033a)
Body > 1 MiB without Content-Length (streaming / chunked)400https://ferra.rs/errors/validation (single errors[0].code = "invalid_json")FerraJson<T>::from_request surfacing as FerraError::Validation

When Content-Length is present, RequestBodyLimitLayer short-circuits at the layer level before the stream is consumed — hence the early 413. When the header is absent, the stream is consumed up to the cap, the read fails, and the JSON extractor rejects the request as a parse error (still machine-readable, still RFC 7807, still parseable via the same generic type-dispatch path you use for the other validation failures).

Both outcomes are semantically correct — the oversized input is rejected either way. The divergence is intentional; a regression test pins the 400 fallback, so any change to it is visible. If you can set Content-Length on your client, do — your clients then see a single, predictable 413.

Other diagnostics

  • 413 with application/problem+json body — request body exceeds 1 MiB. Split the request or raise the limit via FerraLayer::body_limit(...) (Foundry).
  • 429 with Retry-After — peer IP hit the mutation rate limit (2 per second, burst 5 by default). Back off for the number of seconds in Retry-After.
  • problem+json with type: ".../validation" and errors[0].code = "invalid_path_param" — the path segment after /{resource}/ is not a valid primary key for M (e.g. GET /films/abc when Film.id: i32). The built-in path extractor rejects before the handler runs.
  • 500 with detail: "internal server error" — the DB surfaced an error the framework does not map. Inspect logs / tracing for the Debug form of FerraError::Internal; the HTTP body intentionally says nothing more.
  • CORS preflight fails — CorsLayer::new() denies all cross-origin by default. Open it with FerraLayer::cors(...) (Foundry § Transport-layer overrides).

  1. emitted by a middleware mapper (the 413 body-limit mapper or the 429 rate-limit mapper), not by FerraError::IntoResponse. The wire shape is identical to the handler-produced variants — a client that handles one type URI handles them all through the same generic RFC 7807 code path. ↩ ↩2

Projections and routing

The 0.6.5 Chasing deliverable. A #[derive(FerraModel)] struct can expose multiple distinct read/write shapes — projections — by adding a single attribute. Each named projection auto-mounts under its own URL prefix and surfaces as a distinct path in the OpenAPI document, a distinct call in the generated SDK, and a distinct HAL _links.self.href target.

This page is the authoritative user-guide for projection-driven routing. A reader with only this page plus standard Rust knowledge produces a working projection declaration on the first attempt — no ADR and no framework source is required.

Mental model

A projection is a content variant of a resource — not an access-control mechanism. The same underlying row can be served through several projections, each one a deliberate slice of the row’s fields plus a deliberate stance on which fields a client may submit.

The defining property is that every projection is a distinct callable entity at every layer of the stack: a distinct URL path, a distinct OpenAPI operationId, a distinct generated-SDK method, a distinct HAL self link. A consumer that has the URL has, by construction, also fixed the wire shape — there is no header, no query parameter, and no out-of-band negotiation required.

A response is serialized from the projection’s own read struct ({Model}{Name}ReadProjection), not from the row with some keys removed afterwards: a field the projection does not list is not in that struct, so it cannot be in the response. A write_only field and the deletion column of a soft-delete model are in no read struct, and the dispatcher refuses an object that holds the deletion column’s name (0.13.0).

The links of a row follow the route that served it (0.13.0): a row served under /admin/films links to /admin/films/{id} and /admin/films, a page under that prefix links to its own pages, and no link ever points at another projection. POST /admin/films answers with Location: /admin/films/{id}, the row’s self link; a caller who may create but not read the row gets 201 with no body and no Location. A link is present only if following it, as the same caller, answers 2xx; a served row is live, so it has no restore link.

Authorisation is enforced separately — by middleware on the route or by per-operation guards. A detail projection is not an admin-only projection; it is a more detailed projection that a developer may choose to gate behind an authorisation layer if they wish.

The routing contract

SurfaceURLWire shape
Default read (always emitted)GET /{resource}/{id} and GET /{resource}Every readable field of M
Default write (always emitted)POST /{resource}, PUT /{resource}/{id}Every writable field of M
Named projection — auto-derived prefixGET /{name}/{resource}/{id} (etc.)Exactly the fields the projection’s read/write lists declare
