Three refusals come after the statement, because they need the row as written: the authority’s post-write 403, an authority error at the post-check (500), and a storage refusal (a unique 409, a foreign-key violation). before_save has run, its writes are rolled back with the statement, and after_save does not run (Hooks).

authorize = <rule> uses the same grammar as the model’s rules, except that IsOwner is refused (FRG-118): the rule is checked once per request, before any row is read. authorize = inherit declares that the model’s rules suffice. Before 0.13.0 the key was refused (FRG-105, retired): it used to be parsed and dropped.

Field rules

A field can carry its own rule: #[field(read = <rule>)] says who may read it, #[field(write = <rule>)] who may write it (0.13.0). The grammar is the model’s, and IsOwner is allowed in a read rule only (a create has no owner yet, FRG-120). A field with no read rule is readable by everyone who can read the row, and one with no write rule is writable by everyone who can write it: a field with only a write rule is not hidden from readers.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "employees")]
#[ferra(auth = "bearer")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub name: String,
    #[field(read = HasRole("hr") | IsAdmin, write = HasRole("payroll"))]
    pub salary: Option<i64>,
    #[field(read = IsOwner | IsAdmin)]
    pub phone: Option<String>,
    #[field(owner)]
    pub owner_id: Uuid,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

Reads. A field the caller may not read is absent from every response: an item, a list, a create, an update, a restore. It is never null; null means the column is null and the caller may read it. An IsOwner rule is judged on each row alone, from the owner column already loaded (no query), so a list of rows of several owners shows each caller the fields of its own rows. A row whose owner is NULL has no owner. A field in two projections carries the same rule in both.

Writes. The body of a POST or a PUT is judged key by key, after the row is found (404), in this order:

The key sent is…Answer
unknown, outside the write projection, read_only, or a field the caller may not read422, the same unknown_field entry for each, byte for byte as for a key that does not exist
readable, but its write rule refuses the caller403, the fixed body, no field named
readable and writablevalidated and written

One body that triggers several refusals gets the first of these (404, then 422, then 403), and nothing is written. The 422 lists the unknown and the unreadable keys together, sorted by JSON name, so the list never says which kind a key is. On a create the creator owns the row, so an IsOwner read rule never refuses the caller the field it sends.

A gated field that a body omits is left alone: a PUT keeps the column as it is, for every caller (a nullable field without a rule is still reset to NULL by a PUT that omits it, and a required one is a 422, as before), and a POST leaves it to its database default instead of writing NULL. Sending null sets it to NULL.

Filter and sort. A filter[f] or a sort=f on a field the caller may not read is refused as the same parameter on a field that is not filterable or sortable: same status, same body, and the allowed list names only the fields that caller may read. Without that, filter[salary][gt]=… would count the rows above a salary for a caller who may not read it. Through Resource::list and list_cursor the filter is refused alike, and a sort on such a field leaves the default order. A rule that cannot take effect is a compile error (FRG-119), and so is a rule on a field a write projection requires (FRG-133): make such a field Option<T>.

Programmatic authority — #[ferra(authority)]

#[authorize(...)] covers what a rule can say about the caller and the row’s owner. When access depends on something else (the team in a claim, a header, a column of the row), write the decision as code. The model opts in with #[ferra(authority)] and the application supplies two traits, which name no Sea-ORM, axum or http type:

  • FerraAuthority::can(ctx, op, row): may the caller perform op on this row? Called for get, update, delete and restore on the loaded row, and for create on the row as inserted; update is also checked on the row as written. Never called on a list.
  • FerraListAuthority::filter(ctx): the rows the caller may list, as a Condition (below). A model that serves list must implement it (FRG-126): a list with no condition would show every row. Keep it equal to what can allows for get: never more, never less (Writing can and filter).

Both are synchronous and take the RequestContext (who the caller is: subject(), claims::<C>(), header(..)), and both return Result<_, AuthorityError>; an Err or a panic refuses the request (the status is in the table under Writes), and the reason reaches the log, never a response body.

The authority adds to the declared rules, it never replaces them: the posture and #[authorize] run first, unchanged, and an authority that answers true does not override their 401, 403 or 404.

The context is filled from the credential the request carries when the Foundry has .with_auth(), also on an auth = "none" model: a valid token gives the authority its claims, an invalid one is a 401 before can or filter run. Without .with_auth() the context is anonymous (no subject, no claims) whatever the caller sent.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use ferra::authority::{AuthorityError, FerraAuthority, FerraListAuthority};
use ferra::condition::Condition;
use ferra::meta::Operation;
use ferra::request_context::RequestContext;

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "team_docs")]
#[ferra(auth = "bearer", authority)]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub team_id: i64,
    pub title: String,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}

/// The team of the caller, read from the claims `with_auth::<MyClaims>(..)` verified.
struct MyClaims {
    team_id: i64,
}

fn team(ctx: &RequestContext) -> Option<i64> {
    ctx.claims::<MyClaims>().map(|claims| claims.team_id)
}

impl FerraAuthority for Model {
    fn can(ctx: &RequestContext, _op: Operation, row: &Self) -> Result<bool, AuthorityError> {
        Ok(team(ctx) == Some(row.team_id))
    }
}

impl FerraListAuthority for Model {
    fn filter(ctx: &RequestContext) -> Result<Condition<Self>, AuthorityError> {
        Ok(team(ctx).map_or_else(Condition::nothing, |team| Model::FIELDS.team_id.eq(team)))
    }
}
}

Without the key the derive writes a FerraAuthority that allows everything, so an impl FerraAuthority on a model that lacks the key is E0119; the key without the impl is FRG-128.

Writing can and filter

  • Keep filter equal to can(Get). Never more: a list would show a row that get refuses. Never less: after a write, a row can(Get) allows but filter hides still gets a self link, and following it answers 404. Ferra does not check this; test that a list and a get agree for each kind of caller.
  • Keep both pure. The same context and row give the same answer, with no write, no clock and no call out of the process. filter is called more than once per request (on the row lock, again for the links of the response), so a filter that is not pure gives answers that differ inside one request; can runs inside the write’s transaction.
  • Put no secret in an AuthorityError. Its text goes to the log, never to a response body, but a log is where secrets leak. The same holds for the message of a panic.
  • panic = "abort" defeats the guard. Ferra catches a panic in can and filter and refuses the request as it does for an Err; with panic = "abort" in the release profile the process ends instead. The default panic hook writes the message to stderr, outside Ferra’s log.
  • Write both. Every model serves list (a rule set names all five operations, FRG-101), so FerraListAuthority is required (FRG-126) and filter runs on lists, item reads and write locks; can narrows inside it.

Conditions with Model::FIELDS

A Condition is data, built only from the typed handles of Model::FIELDS (one per scalar column), so a column name or a value type cannot be wrong at run time. Ferra turns it into SQL with bound values; there is no LIKE, no subquery, no join.

Model::FIELDS is a {Model}Fields struct (ModelFields for a Model) the derive generates next to the model: that name is reserved in the model’s module, so do not declare a type of the same name there.

  • A handle compares: eq, ne, lt, lte, gt, gte (the value is anything Into the column’s type) and is_in (any iterator of values). On an Option column the comparisons take the inner type, and NULL is reached only through is_null and is_not_null. SQL comparisons never match NULL, which can only make a condition narrower.
  • Condition::all, any and not combine, everything and nothing are the constants. An empty all is everything; an empty any, and an is_in of no value, are nothing.
  • The column types are i32, i64, f64, bool, String, Uuid, Id, DateTime, Date and Time. A computed field and a JSON field have no handle, and neither has the deletion column of a soft-delete model (nor the timestamp and blame columns a behavior owns): a condition cannot reach deleted rows.
  • Bounds: 1 000 values in one is_in, 10 000 in the whole condition, 32 levels deep. A condition over a bound is refused (AuthorityError::TooManyValues, TooDeep), never truncated.
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use ferra::condition::Condition;

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "team_docs")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub team_id: i64,
    pub archived_at: Option<String>,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}

fn visible_to(teams: Vec<i64>) -> Condition<Model> {
    Condition::all([
        Model::FIELDS.team_id.is_in(teams),
        Model::FIELDS.archived_at.is_null(),
    ])
}
fn main() {}

Lists and links

filter is joined by AND to the owner scope and the soft-delete condition, before the page is cut, so the items, total, every offset page and both directions of a cursor walk see the same rows. A condition that matches nothing is a 200 with an empty page and total: 0, never a 403 or a 404. can is never called on a list. When filter returns an Err, panics or is over a bound, the list is a 500 internal with one error! (the model and the operation, no row value, no header), never an empty page: an empty answer would look like a list with no rows.

The links of a get or a list response are decided by the declared rules, can is never called to build one. A list item carries self and collection is present only when filter answers. That is exact as long as filter never matches more than can allows for get (the rule above) and never less: a row can(Get) allows but filter hides still gets a self link, and following it answers 404. Keep filter equal to what can allows for get.

Writes

create, update and restore run the authority inside the write’s transaction. An update reads the row twice, like a Postgres USING / WITH CHECK pair: can(Update) on the row as it is (a refusal is the absent row, 404), then on the row as written, after the UPDATE and before the commit, so a caller of team 1 cannot move a row to team 2 by writing team_id = 2. create judges the row as inserted. restore judges the row before only: filter cannot name the deletion column.

RequestThe authority saysAnswer
GET, PUT, DELETE, POST …/restore on /m/{id}filter excludes the row, or can is false404, the same bytes as an absent row; the row is unchanged
PUT /m/{id}the row is allowed, can(Update) is false on the row as written403 forbidden, rolled back
POST /mcan(Create) is false on the inserted row403 forbidden, nothing written
a row operationErr or a panic404 as above, one error!
POST /m, the update post-check, GET /mErr or a panic500 internal, one error!, rolled back
POST /m, PUT /m/{id}a unique constraint is violated409 conflict, before the 403

The 409 comes first because the database refuses the value before can sees the row, so a caller can learn that a row it may not see holds a value. Make every unique constraint per tenant: a composite index with the column the authority scopes by (UNIQUE (team_id, slug), not UNIQUE (slug)).

The self link of a create, update or restore response also needs can(Get) on the row as returned, called once in memory after the commit. A write-only authority (can(Create) is true, can(Get) is false) gets 201 with no body and no Location, and 204 with an empty body on update and restore, whatever Prefer and Accept say: the row is written and nothing of it is sent. An Err or a panic in that call answers the same, with one error!, never a 500: the write has happened, and a client that retries would write it twice. On a model that serves list, a row can(Get) allows but filter hides gets a self that answers 404; keep filter equal to what can allows for get.

Request context

An authority and a hook read the request through a RequestContext (ferra::request_context::RequestContext, full reference in ferra-core.md):

AccessorAnswers
subject()the caller’s FerraIdentity::id(), None when anonymous
is_authenticated(), has_role(&str)a verified identity is present; it holds that role
claims::<C>()the claims of a bearer or cookie token, as the type given to .with_auth::<C>()
api_key()the identity of the API key that authenticated the request
header(&str)the first value of a request header, case-insensitive
  • claims::<C>() is None on a mismatch. An API key request, an anonymous one, and a C other than the .with_auth type all answer None: check it, and refuse when you needed the claims.
  • Credentials are not there. Authorization, Proxy-Authorization, Cookie and the Foundry’s API key header are dropped when the context is built, in any case: header("Authorization") is None, and Debug prints the subject and the header names, never a value.
  • Every other header is the client’s. header("X-Team") returns what the caller sent. Never authorize on X-Forwarded-*, Forwarded, Host or Origin: a client can set them, unless a proxy of yours overwrites them before the request reaches Ferra. Decide from the claims, which are signed.
  • Anonymous without .with_auth(). The context then has no subject and no claims, whatever the request carried.
  • Not Copy. .clone() it where 0.12 copied it (migration note).
use ferra::request_context::RequestContext;

struct MyClaims {
    team_id: i64,
}

fn caller_team(ctx: &RequestContext) -> Option<i64> {
    // `None` for an anonymous caller, an API key, or claims of another type.
    ctx.claims::<MyClaims>().map(|claims| claims.team_id)
}
fn main() {}

Compile-time auth defense

Three compile-time gates stand between a model and an unprotected route.

  1. At the model declaration — FRG-100. A model with neither #[ferra(auth = ...)] nor an #[authorize(...)] block does not compile. The error proposes, in order: auth = "bearer" with .with_auth::<YourClaims>(jwt), auth = "none" for a deliberately public model, or an #[authorize(...)] block.

  2. At the mount call site — FRG-150. Foundry::mount::<M>() requires M: FerraAuthConfigured, which #[derive(FerraModel)] implements for every model that declares a posture. It catches a hand-written FerraModel impl without one.

  3. At the mount call site — FRG-151. A model whose rules need an identity — auth = "bearer", or any rule other than Anyone, a projection’s authorize and a field’s read / write rule included — cannot be mounted on a chain without .with_auth():

    error[E0277]: FRG-151: `Film` requires an identity, but this `Foundry` chain has no `.with_auth()`

    The bad call is Foundry::new(conn).mount::<Film>().build(); the good one names the claims type (both, compiled, under FRG-151):

    use ferra::{FerraIdentity, FerraModel, Foundry, JwtConfig};
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "bearer")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Deserialize)]
struct MyClaims { sub: String }
impl FerraIdentity for MyClaims {
    fn id(&self) -> &str { &self.sub }
    fn has_role(&self, _role: &str) -> bool { false }
}
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection, jwt: JwtConfig) {
let app = Foundry::new(conn).with_auth::<MyClaims>(jwt).mount::<Film>().build();
let _ = app;
}
fn main() {}

    A model declared auth = "none", or whose #[authorize] rules are all Anyone, mounts on any chain.

Declarations that used to compile and enforce nothing are refused:

DeclarationSince 0.9.0
#[ferra(projection(..., authorize = ...))] (refused 0.9.0 to 0.12.x)FRG-105, retired in 0.13.0 — valid again, see § Projections and authorization
#[ferra(exposure = "auto_*")]FRG-106 — see ferra-forge.md § Removed in 0.9.0: exposure
#[authorize()] (empty)FRG-101
#[authorize(get = AuthRule::IsAdmin, ...)] (qualified checker)FRG-103 — write the bare IsAdmin
#[authorize(update = HasRole(""), ...)] (empty or blank role)FRG-101 — name the role
#[operation(...)]FRG-335 — see behaviors.md

At runtime, Foundry::build() refuses to start (FRG-150) if a mounted model leaves an operation without a rule — a hand-written FerraModel impl is the only way to get there.

Error responses

SituationStatustype URI
No token where an identity is required401 + WWW-Authenticate: Bearerhttps://ferra.rs/errors/unauthorized
Token present but invalid — bad signature, expired, not yet valid (nbf), unknown kid, critical header, claims that will not deserialise, iss/aud mismatch401 + WWW-Authenticate: Bearerhttps://ferra.rs/errors/unauthorized
Two or more credentials (an Authorization header, an API key and the cookie, two of any, or two of one), whatever they hold400https://ferra.rs/errors/multiple_credentials
API key refused — unknown prefix, wrong secret, revoked, expired, malformed401 + WWW-Authenticate: Bearerhttps://ferra.rs/errors/unauthorized
Key set or key store out of reach (no fresh key cached, database down)503https://ferra.rs/errors/identity_unavailable
Valid token, but the operation’s predicate returned false403https://ferra.rs/errors/forbidden
Write authenticated by the cookie, Origin missing, null, repeated or not listed (Cookie)403https://ferra.rs/errors/forbidden (its own fixed detail)
Valid token, the row belongs to someone else (IsOwner rule)404https://ferra.rs/errors/not_found

The 401/403 split is load-bearing and worth stating plainly: 401 means the framework could not establish who you are; 403 means it knows exactly who you are and the answer is still no. A 403 is therefore positive evidence that your token was accepted.

A present-but-invalid token is refused 401 even on an operation whose rule is Anyone — presenting a broken credential is a failed authentication attempt, which is a different event from not presenting one at all. A tokenless request to an Anyone operation is served normally.

That rule only applies to models that wired the layer at all. On a model whose every rule is Anyone (or that declares auth = "none"), there is no layer, so nothing inspects the header and a broken token is simply ignored. The behaviour of an Anyone operation therefore depends on what its sibling operations declare: add update = IsOwner to an otherwise-public model and a stale token starts 401-ing on list, which previously ignored it. Worth knowing before you tighten one operation on a live model.

403 responses do not carry WWW-Authenticate — that header is an authentication challenge, and the authentication already succeeded.

All bodies are application/problem+json (RFC 9457):

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/forbidden",
  "title": "Forbidden",
  "status": 403,
  "detail": "forbidden"
}

None of them ever echo token bytes, decoded claims, kid values, or the row’s owner value — not in detail, not in instance, not in an extension field. Each carries a fixed, framework-authored detail string.

That last property has a client-side cost worth planning for: the six distinct 401 causes (no token, bad signature, expired, unknown kid, undeserialisable claims, iss/aud mismatch) are deliberately indistinguishable on the wire, and the WWW-Authenticate value carries no RFC 6750 error parameter. A client cannot tell “expired, refresh and retry” from “misconfigured, retrying will never work” — so cap automatic refresh-and-replay at one attempt rather than looping.

A row you may not see returns 404, not 403. When an IsOwner rule refuses a row that belongs to someone else, the answer is the 404 a missing row gets, byte for byte, so the caller cannot learn that the row exists. A 403 remains the answer for a model rule that does not depend on ownership (IsAdmin, HasRole("…")), or when the caller owns the row but fails another part of the rule (IsOwner + HasRole("editor")); a caller that the rule of the projection under a prefix refuses gets the 404 first (see Projections and authorization). A soft-deleted row is a 404 on get, update and delete; restore reads it on purpose and applies the same 404 rule.

Where auth sits in the request pipeline

Outermost first, as a request traverses it:

CORS  →  auth  →  body-size limit  →  tracing  →  route  →  rate limit (mutations)
      →  handler: #[authorize] check  →  body parse  →  validation  →  database

Two consequences worth planning around:

  • Authentication precedes body parsing and validation. An unauthenticated caller gets 401 without the framework reading their body, so probing for schema shape through validation errors requires a valid token first.
  • The per-operation #[authorize] check runs inside the handler, before the body is parsed. An unauthorised caller never receives validation detail about a resource they may not touch.

CORS answers the preflight before authentication runs. A browser sends OPTIONS with no Authorization header — the Fetch spec forbids attaching one — so the CORS layer sits outside the auth layer and answers the preflight itself; the request never reaches authentication. Without that order every browser client of a bearer-protected model would break on the preflight, before the real request was ever sent. The same order lets a listed origin read the 401, 400 and 403 of the layers inside.

The preflight is answered with headers only, and it cannot reach a CRUD handler because the routes register GET/POST/PUT/DELETE, so any other OPTIONS falls through to 405.

Note that Ferra’s default CORS posture is restrictive (CorsLayer::new() denies all cross-origin). Reaching a browser client takes an explicit CORS configuration through FerraLayer — see foundry.md.

Testing authenticated routes

A test goes through the same JWT layer as production: it sends a real token, signed with the secret of its own test configuration. ferra::testing::bearer signs one and returns the Authorization header value — no JWT crate to add to your project:

use ferra::testing::bearer;
use ferra::{ClaimCheck, Foundry, HmacAlgorithm, JwtConfig};
use ferra::{FerraIdentity, FerraModel};
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod article {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "articles")]
    #[ferra(auth = "bearer")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
#[derive(Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct MyClaims {
    pub sub: String,
    pub roles: Vec<String>,
    pub exp: usize,
}
impl FerraIdentity for MyClaims {
    fn id(&self) -> &str { &self.sub }
    fn has_role(&self, role: &str) -> bool { self.roles.iter().any(|r| r == role) }
}

const KID: &str = "test-key";
const SECRET: &str = "test-secret-test-secret-test-secret!";

// HS256 needs a secret of at least 32 bytes. The test tokens carry no `iss`
// and no `aud`: say so. With `ClaimCheck::expect(...)`, put the claim in them.
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
let jwt = JwtConfig::single_secret(KID, SECRET.to_owned(), HmacAlgorithm::Hs256, ClaimCheck::Skip, ClaimCheck::Skip)?;
let app = Foundry::new(conn).with_auth::<MyClaims>(jwt).mount::<article::Model>().build();

let alice = MyClaims { sub: "0190a4a0-0000-7000-8000-0000000000a1".into(), roles: vec![], exp: 4_102_444_800 };
let authorization = bearer(KID, SECRET, HmacAlgorithm::Hs256, &alice)?; // "Bearer eyJ…"
// send requests with `.header("authorization", &authorization)`
let _ = (app, authorization);
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

bearer(kid, secret, algorithm, &claims) takes your own claims type (anything Serialize) and returns Result<String, ferra::testing::TokenSigningError>. The token must satisfy the configuration like any other: exp in the future (the value above is 2100-01-01), and the iss / aud the JwtConfig expects, if any. The router you exercise is the real one, JWT layer included.

There is no way to hand the framework an identity without a token. The authorization checkpoint and CurrentUser only trust an identity the layer built from a verified token: neither a test helper nor a middleware of yours can slip one in. bearer is not a bypass — a token signed with another secret is refused — so it needs no Cargo feature and cannot weaken a release build.

Two consequences to know:

  • A custom handler is tested without a token. CurrentUser is a plain tuple struct: call your handler directly with CurrentUser(claims).

    use axum::http::StatusCode;
use ferra::{CurrentUser, FerraError};
#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
struct MyClaims { sub: String }
async fn publish_film(CurrentUser(user): CurrentUser<MyClaims>) -> Result<StatusCode, FerraError> {
    let _ = user.sub;
    Ok(StatusCode::NO_CONTENT)
}
async fn demo(alice: MyClaims) -> Result<(), FerraError> {
let status = publish_film(CurrentUser(alice)).await?;
let _ = status;
Ok(())
}
fn main() {}

  • Ferra’s checkpoint has one source of identity in 0.9.0: its JWT layer, with a shared HMAC secret (HS256, HS384, HS512). You cannot plug another authenticator — an RS256 / JWKS verifier, a session cookie — into the generated routes or into CurrentUser; JWKS is out of scope for 0.9.0. Put such a scheme in front of your own handlers with your own extractor, or exchange its credential for an HMAC token your service signs.

To craft tokens bearer does not produce (a custom header, a broken signature), sign them yourself with the JWT crate Ferra uses, declared exactly like this in [dev-dependencies]:

jsonwebtoken = { version = "11.1", default-features = false, features = ["rust_crypto"] }

Another backend (aws_lc_rs) or another major version leaves jsonwebtoken without a single crypto provider, and the first signature panics with « Could not automatically determine the process-level CryptoProvider ».

  • ferra-error-handling.md — the full typed-error surface and the closed ERROR_TYPES namespace.
  • projections-and-routing.md — projection URLs and field sets; a projection route follows the model’s rules and, with authorize, its own.
  • foundry.md — mounting, versioning, and transport-layer composition.

ferra-openapi

ferra-openapi is the framework’s documentation surface. It builds an OpenAPI 3.2 document from the description of each mounted model and serves it at /docs/openapi.json, plus an interactive Scalar page at /docs. Both are derived end-to-end from the same model that drives the routes, the SQL queries and the hypermedia links.

An application does not declare or call ferra-openapi: the crate has no public API of its own in 0.9. The way in is Foundry::with_docs() (or one of its variants below), and the way out is the running router: you read the document at /docs/openapi.json.

Dependencies. The examples on this page assume the dependencies of Getting started:

[dependencies]
ferra   = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.13.1" }
sea-orm = { version = "2.0", default-features = false, features = ["macros", "runtime-tokio-rustls", "sqlx-postgres"] }
tokio   = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread"] }
axum    = "0.8"
serde   = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }

What you get for free

A Ferra model mounted through Foundry::with_docs() produces:

  • GET /docs/openapi.json — the full OpenAPI 3.2 document (openapi: "3.2.0").
  • GET /docs — interactive Scalar UI rendering the spec.
  • Every answer is documented. Each operation lists the error statuses the server can return for it — 400; 401 when the model reads tokens; 403 when the rule needs an identity; 404 on item routes; 409 on writes; 413 and 422 on bodies; 429 on mutations (not under no_rate_limit()); 500 — each an application/problem+json body. A chain with request_budget adds a 503 to every operation, and a chain whose JWT source is a key set (JwtConfig::key_set), or that accepts API keys (with_api_keys), adds it to the operations of the models that read tokens: all are the one named response ServiceUnavailable of components/responses ($ref to ProblemDetails; its type is timeout or identity_unavailable), never an inline response.
  • API keys are a security scheme. On a chain that accepts API keys, the document declares components/securitySchemes/apiKey (type: apiKey, in: header, name the configured header) and lists it as an alternative to bearer in the security of every operation that requires a credential.
  • The cookie is a security scheme. On a chain whose JwtConfig has with_cookie, the document declares components/securitySchemes/cookie (type: apiKey, in: cookie, name the configured cookie), lists it as an alternative next to bearer, and gives every mutation of a model that reads tokens the named response Forbidden (the 403 of a write whose Origin is not allowed), a $ref to ProblemDetails.
  • Collections match their pagination mode: page (page, per_page, total), cursor (next_cursor, required, a string or null) or both (either shape, as a oneOf that an answer matches one of only, by the keys each requires). These are the flat schemas, without _links.
  • Both representations are declared. Every negotiated 2xx lists application/json (the flat schema) and application/hal+json (the named schema <Model>Hal or <Model>CollectionHal, an allOf of the flat schema and {_links}). The items of a <Model>CollectionHal are <Model>Hal, since each item of a HAL list carries its own _links (0.13.0). In <Model>Hal, _links.self and _links.collection are optional: an item served to a caller who may list but not GET it has no self (0.13.0). A list’s own _links.self stays required.
  • A gated field is declared optional. A field with a #[field(read = …)] rule is never in the required list of its read schema and is described “absent when the caller may not read it”; its examples stay synthetic (a placeholder of its type, never a value of yours). The POST and PUT of a write projection that holds a field with a write rule declare 403, also on a model whose own rules are public (0.13.0).
  • An authority and a parent chain are declared. The POST and PUT of a model with #[ferra(authority)] declare the named 403 (the authority refuses a write with it), also on a model whose own rules are public; on such a model served with .with_auth() every operation declares 401 and the optional bearer requirement, since the layer reads tokens. The 422 of a model with owner(from) names the code reference_not_found in its description (0.13.0).
  • Blame columns are optional. The created_by and updated_by columns of a #[behavior(blameable)] model (under their configured names) are read-only optional strings in every read schema that lists them, described “absent when the caller may not read it”, and in no write schema (0.13.0).
  • A projection rule is declared. Every operation under a projection that carries an authorize rule declares 404 (a caller the rule refuses is told nothing, a list or a create included), and, when the rule needs an identity, 401 and the bearer security requirement (0.13.0).
  • Date filters. A DateTime, Date or Time filter field has filter[f] and filter[f][gt|gte|lt|lte] parameters with the field’s format (date-time, date; a Time has the HH:MM:SS[.fraction] pattern, as its schema does). A cursor-mode sort is an enum of the cursor key and its - form.
  • Projections: every projection route is documented, restore included, and the bare path shows the promoted projection when there is one.
  • Field names are the wire names. On a model that declares #[ferra(rename_all = "camelCase")], schemas, required lists, filter[...] parameters, sort values and examples all use the camelCase names.
  • Ferra’s own test suite checks this contract: every route of every test model is called with a request built from the document, and every answer is validated against it.

Foundry::with_docs() serves both routes to anyone who reaches the port. For any surface a network can reach, use Foundry::with_docs_protected(verifier), which answers an anonymous request with a 401: see Enabling the docs surface.

For each mounted model M (PascalCase struct name), the spec contains:

  • Five paths (GET /{resource}, GET /{resource}/{id}, POST /{resource}, PUT /{resource}/{id}, DELETE /{resource}/{id}).
  • Four projection schemas ({Model}, Create{Model}Input, Update{Model}Input, {Model}Collection).
  • A shared ProblemDetails schema referenced by every error response.
  • Every operation carries an operationId and a tags array containing the resource name. Zero inline schemas in operation definitions; every body schema is a $ref into components/schemas.

Collection operations (0.7.5 Enameling). The GET /{resource} operation’s parameter set is mode-aware: page-mode models emit page + per_page, cursor-mode emits per_page + cursor (with the ferra-cursor format identifier per spec 011 FR-029), and both- mode emits all three with the cursor parameter description quoting the mutual-exclusivity rule (FR-010 / FR-030). Adding a new #[field(filterable)] or #[field(sortable)] to the model automatically widens the OpenAPI filter[…] parameter list and the sort enum on the next emission (FR-032 / FR-033). See pagination.md for the consumer-facing surface.

/me

A model that declares #[ferra(me)] adds one more path, GET /me (under the version prefix: /v1/me), with the operationId getMe and no path parameter. Its responses are 200 (the model’s read schema), 401, 403 (a get rule that reads no row), 404 (every refusal that depends on the row answers it, see projections-and-routing.md § /me), and the 400 and 500 of every generated operation, all as ProblemDetails. The path has no other method.

Enabling the docs surface

For any surface a network can reach, the call site is Foundry::with_docs_protected(verifier): an anonymous request gets a 401 with an RFC 7807 body, and the verifier is yours to write.

use ferra::Foundry;
use axum::http::header::AUTHORIZATION;
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) {
// Constant time: `==` on a secret stops at the first differing byte, and the delay tells it.
fn same(a: &[u8], b: &[u8]) -> bool {
    a.len() == b.len() && a.iter().zip(b).fold(0u8, |acc, (x, y)| acc | (x ^ y)) == 0
}
let docs_token = std::env::var("DOCS_TOKEN").unwrap_or_default();
let app = Foundry::new(conn)
    .mount::<Film>()
    .with_docs_protected(move |req: &axum::extract::Request| {
        let sent = req.headers().get(AUTHORIZATION).map_or(&[][..], |v| v.as_bytes());
        !docs_token.is_empty() && same(sent, format!("Bearer {docs_token}").as_bytes())
    })
    .build();
let _ = app;
}
fn main() {}

Foundry::with_docs() is for a local or internal service, where the inventory is the feature and nobody outside reaches the port:

use ferra::Foundry;
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) {
let app = Foundry::new(conn)
    .mount::<Film>()
    .with_docs()
    .build();
let _ = app;
}
fn main() {}

That single chain produces a runnable HTTP service mounting Film’s five CRUD endpoints plus /docs/openapi.json and /docs with zero boilerplate.

Variants

MethodEffect
.with_docs_protected(verifier)Auth-gated docs at /docs; anonymous requests get 401 + RFC 7807 body.
.with_docs_protected_at("/api-docs", verifier)Auth-gated at the supplied prefix.
.with_docs()Public docs at /docs and /docs/openapi.json, for local or internal use.
.with_docs_at("/api-docs")Public docs at the supplied prefix.

Title, version and security

The document’s info.title and info.version are "API" and "1" unless you set them; the Scalar page uses the same title:

use ferra::{FerraIdentity, Foundry, JwtConfig};
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod article {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "articles")]
    #[ferra(auth = "bearer")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Deserialize)]
struct MyClaims { sub: String }
impl FerraIdentity for MyClaims {
    fn id(&self) -> &str { &self.sub }
    fn has_role(&self, _role: &str) -> bool { false }
}
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection, jwt: JwtConfig) {
let app = Foundry::new(conn)
    .with_auth::<MyClaims>(jwt)
    .mount::<article::Model>()
    .with_docs()
    .with_docs_info("Films API", "2026.10")
    .build();
let _ = app;
}
fn main() {}

When a mounted model reads tokens, the document declares an HTTP bearer scheme named bearer (bearerFormat: JWT) in components.securitySchemes, and each operation says what it needs: security: [{"bearer": []}] when its rule needs an identity, [{}, {"bearer": []}] when a token is optional. The routes of with_docs() stay public; with_docs_protected gates them.

Every schema property carries examples (a one-element array: the Schema Object’s example keyword is deprecated since OpenAPI 3.1), every request body, parameter and header an example, and error responses are shared components.responses (BadRequest, Unauthorized, Forbidden, NotFound, Conflict, PayloadTooLarge, ValidationError, TooManyRequests, InternalServerError).

The document is built once, at Foundry::build(). If Ferra cannot finish it — a Ferra bug — build() panics with an explicit message rather than serve a document that silently lost part of its content.

Response headers of the docs page

The page loads one script, cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@scalar/api-reference@1.72.2/dist/browser/standalone.js, pinned to that file and checked by its Subresource Integrity hash, and fonts from fonts.scalar.com. A deployment that cannot reach those hosts gets no page; the document at /docs/openapi.json is served by your own process and is not affected.

Scalar’s telemetry and its agent tool are disabled in the served page, and Scalar’s request proxy (proxyUrl) is not set. The headers keep the page from reaching anything else, whatever a later Scalar default becomes:

  • GET /docs (the page; /api-docs with with_docs_at("/api-docs"); public or protected) sends
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@scalar/api-reference@1.72.2/dist/browser/standalone.js; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; font-src https://fonts.scalar.com data:; img-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'self'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'
  • every response the docs routes produce (the HTML page, the JSON document, the protected variant’s 401) sends X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff. Only the HTML page sends the policy above: the 401 and the JSON document carry nosniff and no Content-Security-Policy. The 503 of the request budget is built outside the header layer of the docs routes and carries neither.

Ferra sets these two headers on the docs routes, inside the Foundry’s request-budget and cache layers, which leave them as set. Your own policy: a second Content-Security-Policy header added by an outer layer or a proxy is enforced together with Ferra’s, the stricter wins for each directive; a layer or proxy that overwrites the header replaces Ferra’s policy, and then the page is only as strict as yours.

Why the inventory is generated

The framework’s default-deny posture on model routes does not extend to with_docs(), which has no gate: it is meant for a local or internal service, where the inventory is the feature.

/docs/openapi.json is generated from the same ModelMeta IR that drives the routes. By construction, every endpoint a Ferra application exposes is documented, with no manual schema to keep in sync. This structurally closes OWASP API Security Top 10 API9:2023 (Improper Inventory Management) — the gap between the API a team thinks it exposes and the API actually deployed. Salt Security research cited in OWASP API9 measures that gap at 40% on average in production (one cited case: 54 undocumented endpoints, 12 exposing PII). The same document is also a map of the surface for whoever reads it, so who may read it is a choice: .with_docs_protected(verifier) gates the surface behind your verifier, and the inventory stays complete for the operators you let in.

Rule of thumb: prefer .with_docs_protected(verifier) for any surface a network can reach, and keep .with_docs() for local development and internal tools, where the inventory is the feature. The examples hello-ferra and movie-stars use .with_docs() for local development and listen on every interface (0.0.0.0:3000), so their page is public to anyone who can reach the port; examples/lambda-neon, the one that is deployed, mounts no documentation page and answers /docs like any unknown path.

The deviation from default-deny is recorded in ADR-0024 for the curious reader; this guide stands alone.

Naming conventions

Schema names

For a model named Film with no named projections declared, the spec carries four entries in components/schemas:

ProjectionOpenAPI schema namePurpose
ReadFilmResponse shape for GET and the body of POST / PUT responses.
CreateCreateFilmInputRequest body of POST /films.
UpdateUpdateFilmInputRequest body of PUT /films/{id}.
CollectionFilmCollectionResponse shape for GET /films ({ items: [Film], page, per_page, total }).

The schema name derives from resource_name (the URL path slug) via PascalCase singularisation.

Per-projection schemas

A model that declares one or more #[ferra(projection(...))] blocks emits four additional schemas per named projection (read, create, update and collection), plus the HAL forms of its read and collection schemas. For Film with one named admin projection (#[ferra(projection(name = "admin", read = […], write = […]))]):

ProjectionOpenAPI schema nameOperations served at
ReadFilmAdminGET /admin/films/{id}, GET /admin/films
CreateCreateFilmAdminInputPOST /admin/films
UpdateUpdateFilmAdminInputPUT /admin/films/{id}
CollectionFilmAdminCollectionGET /admin/films (pagination envelope)

The general rule:

  • Read schema: {Model}{Projection-PascalCase}.
  • Create schema: Create{Model}{Projection-PascalCase}Input.
  • Update schema: Update{Model}{Projection-PascalCase}Input.

For the default projection the {Projection-PascalCase} segment is the empty string, so the rule produces Film, CreateFilmInput, UpdateFilmInput.

{Model} is the singular of the resource name (films gives Film), never the Rust struct ident, which is Model in every Sea-ORM entity. The resource name is the one #[ferra(resource = "...")] gives, else the default of ferra-forge.md: the #[sea_orm(table_name)] literal, else a plural of the struct ident. The operationId of a projection’s route ends in the same {Projection-PascalCase} (getFilmAdmin, listFilmsAdmin), so it is not the default’s. Two models that name a projection alike keep a schema each.

A system_only model serves no write, so its document carries the Read and Collection schemas only (and their HAL forms), with no Create or Update schema, for the default projection and for each named one.

Each schema’s properties map carries exactly the field set the corresponding projection declares — no schema reuse via $ref from one projection to another. A reader scanning the document sees the per-projection shape without dereferencing chains.

Names are SDK-friendly: orval, openapi-generator, kiota, and their peers produce idiomatic, distinguishable types in the target language without post-processing. The framework’s internal Rust struct names (FilmReadProjection, FilmAdminReadProjection, …) NEVER leak into the published document — components/schemas keys, $ref values, operation IDs, and descriptions all carry only the public names from the tables above.

x-ferra-promoted-in vendor extension

When a named projection carries default = true with a breaking_change_version = "X.Y.Z" attestation (per ADR-0030 §Default-projection promotion safeguards), every operation served under the bare resource path gains an x-ferra-promoted-in: "X.Y.Z" vendor extension. SDK generators and downstream tooling (ferra anvil) surface the silent breaking change to consumers who might otherwise see only the URL stability.

operationId

Every operation carries a stable operationId:

MethodPathoperationId
GET/filmslistFilms
GET/films/{id}getFilm
POST/filmscreateFilm
PUT/films/{id}updateFilm
DELETE/films/{id}deleteFilm

The list id is list and the plural of the model name, made as the derive makes a resource name: Category gives listCategories, Box gives listBoxes, Film gives listFilms.

Versioned chains (Foundry::api_version("v1")) prefix the operationId with the version segment: v1.listFilms, v1.getFilm, etc.

tags

Every operation carries a single tag — the resource name in snake_case plural (films, actors). Scalar / Redoc / Swagger UI group operations by tag for easier navigation.

Field type mapping

Field types map to OpenAPI 3.2 schemas as follows:

Rust typeOpenAPI
String{ "type": "string" }
i32{ "type": "integer", "format": "int32" }
i64{ "type": "integer", "format": "int64" }
f32 / f64{ "type": "number" }
bool{ "type": "boolean" }
ferra::Id / Uuid{ "type": "string", "format": "uuid" }
Option<T>nullable T ({ "type": ["string", "null"] }) and absent from required
ferra::DateTime{ "type": "string", "format": "date-time" }
ferra::Date{ "type": "string", "format": "date" }
ferra::Time{ "type": "string", "pattern": "^([01][0-9]|2[0-3]):[0-5][0-9]:[0-5][0-9](\\.[0-9]{1,9})?$" }

Option<T> uses the nullable form of OpenAPI 3.1 and later (a type array containing "null"), not the 3.0 nullable: true keyword.

The three typed time newtypes (ferra::DateTime, ferra::Date, ferra::Time) are recognised by the framework and emit the right format. Direct use of legacy time crates (chrono::*, time::*, jiff::*) is rejected at the field-declaration site — see the §“Time vocabulary” section of ferra-core.md.

Field annotations

Four attributes shape what appears in each projection: #[ferra(skip)], #[ferra(read_only)], #[ferra(write_only)] and #[ferra(computed)].

#[ferra(skip)]

Excludes the field from every projection schema and from the wire contract. Useful for server-only state (audit timestamps, internal flags).

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub title: String,
    #[ferra(skip)]
    pub internal_note: String,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

internal_note does not appear in Film, CreateFilmInput, or UpdateFilmInput, and the wire shape rejects an inbound value for that field.

#[ferra(read_only)]

The field appears in every read schema (Film and any per-projection read schema where the field is included) marked readOnly: true, and is structurally absent from every create / update input schema. Useful for server-assigned values that the consumer can read but cannot write.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub title: String,
    #[ferra(read_only)]
    pub indexed_at: ferra::DateTime,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

indexed_at appears in Film with readOnly: true; both CreateFilmInput and UpdateFilmInput omit the property entirely. If the model also declares a named admin projection that includes indexed_at in its read = [...] list, the field appears in FilmAdmin with readOnly: true and is omitted from CreateFilmAdminInput / UpdateFilmAdminInput.

#[ferra(write_only)]

The field appears in every write schema (CreateFilmInput / UpdateFilmInput / per-projection input schemas where the field is included), and is structurally absent from every read schema — not marked writeOnly: true on the read side, but simply missing. Useful for fields the consumer must supply on write but should never see on read (one-shot secrets, transient hints, write-side credentials).

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub title: String,
    #[ferra(write_only)]
    pub new_password: String,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

new_password appears in CreateFilmInput and UpdateFilmInput; the Film read schema omits the property entirely. The framework guarantees the field cannot leak via a read operation — its absence is enforced at compile time on the generated read-projection struct.

#[ferra(computed)]

The field is server-derived (e.g., a derived count, a denormalised projection of joined rows). It appears in every read schema with readOnly: true, and is structurally absent from every write input schema — the framework calls FerraComputed::compute() / compute_async_batch() on read and never accepts the field as inbound input.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub title: String,
    #[sea_orm(ignore)]
    #[ferra(computed)]
    pub review_count: i64,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
impl ferra::compute::FerraComputed for Model {} // the default `compute` leaves the value as it is
}

review_count appears in Film with readOnly: true; the create and update inputs omit the property entirely. See ferra-core.md § Computed fields for the FerraComputed trait that drives the compute pipeline.

The shared ProblemDetails schema

Every error response in the spec references the same schema:

{
  "$ref": "#/components/schemas/ProblemDetails"
}

The schema’s body:

{
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["type", "title", "status"],
  "properties": {
    "type":   {
      "type": "string",
      "format": "uri",
      "enum": [
        "https://ferra.rs/errors/not_found",
        "https://ferra.rs/errors/validation",
        "https://ferra.rs/errors/conflict",
        "https://ferra.rs/errors/internal",
        "https://ferra.rs/errors/payload_too_large",
        "https://ferra.rs/errors/rate_limited",
        "https://ferra.rs/errors/unauthorized",
        "https://ferra.rs/errors/validation_failed",
        "https://ferra.rs/errors/invalid_cursor",
        "https://ferra.rs/errors/forbidden",
        "https://ferra.rs/errors/unsupported_media_type",
        "https://ferra.rs/errors/timeout"
      ]
    },
    "title":    { "type": "string" },
    "status":   { "type": "integer", "format": "int32" },
    "detail":   { "type": "string" },
    "instance": { "type": "string", "format": "uri-reference" }
  }
}

The closed enum on type is the load-bearing constraint: SDK generators produce a typed union over the URI set in the target language. An AI agent generating client code is foreclosed from fabricating new URIs — values outside the enum fail schema validation.

The full URI table (with HTTP status, title, and example body for every variant) lives in error handling.

Mounting an alternative UI

/docs/openapi.json is the framework’s stable spec endpoint; the Scalar UI at /docs is the bundled default but not the only choice. To use Redoc, RapiDoc or Swagger UI, serve it yourself and point it at /docs/openapi.json, which with_docs() mounts. ferra-openapi has no public API since 0.9.0: the document is reached through the running router, not through a function call.

Where the spec is built

Foundry::build() assembles the full document from the static ModelMeta of every mounted model. It runs once at process startup; the resulting document is cached and served unchanged on every /docs/openapi.json request — no per-request rebuild. Its title and version are set with with_docs_info(title, version).

Linting your spec

Ferra’s CI lints the generated reference document with vacuum 0.30.6 — Spectral cannot read OpenAPI 3.2 — using the workspace’s .spectral.yaml ruleset (Spectral-compatible), at the warn severity bar: any finding blocks the build. The ruleset extends the default OpenAPI rules with four Ferra rules (every operation declares tags and an operationId; request and response body schemas are $refs into components/schemas), and keeps oas3-missing-example and description-duplication on: the document carries an example for every property, body, parameter and header, and no description twice.

vacuum lint -r .spectral.yaml -n warn openapi.json

The same ruleset is a reasonable start for a downstream repository; add deployment rules to it (for example oas3-api-servers once the deployment declares servers).

See also

  • Foundry — the assembly facade that mounts the docs surface alongside resource routes.
  • Error handling — the closed ERROR_TYPES URI namespace and the ProblemDetails consumer- side branching pattern.
  • ferra-core §Time vocabulary — the typed DateTime / Date newtypes that emit format: date-time and format: date in the spec.

For curious readers, the architectural decisions behind the docs surface are recorded in ADR-0024 (crate scope + public-default posture), ADR-0026 (closed ERROR_TYPES URI namespace), and ADR-0003 v2 (Scalar over Swagger UI as the default UI). These ADRs are not load-bearing for correct use of the feature; this guide stands alone.

JSON field schemas

A JSON field’s schema is {}: any JSON value. Supply a function returning a JSON Schema object or boolean with #[field(json(schema = crate::settings_schema))]. The served OpenAPI document inserts the function’s serde_json::Value verbatim; keywords such as const and $defs are retained. Optional JSON fields use anyOf: [<schema>, {"type": "null"}]. Schema overrides describe the API; write validation still follows the Rust type and declared JSON bounds.

ferra-forge — the #[derive(FerraModel)] derive

Reader contract. This page stands on its own. A reader with only this page plus standard Rust and Sea-ORM knowledge can produce a compiling entity on the first attempt. Cross-references to ADRs and the constitution are non-load-bearing — every correctness cue is spelled out below.

ferra-forge is the Ferra proc-macro crate. It exports one procedural derive, #[derive(FerraModel)], which binds a Rust struct to its static ferra::meta::ModelMeta description. The derive cohabits with Sea-ORM’s DeriveEntityModel on the same struct — neither replaces the other; both read the struct.

Dependencies. The examples on this page assume the dependencies of Getting started:

[dependencies]
ferra   = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.13.1" }
sea-orm = { version = "2.0", default-features = false, features = ["macros", "runtime-tokio-rustls", "sqlx-postgres"] }
tokio   = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread"] }
axum    = "0.8"
serde   = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }

Canonical entity shape (sibling-derive)

The canonical entity is a plain Rust struct with six derives and three container attributes (a table, a posture, and optionally more):

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "bearer")] // the posture: `"bearer"`, `"none"`, or an `#[authorize(...)]` block
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub title: String,
    pub release_year: Option<i32>,
    pub rating: f64,
}

// Sea-ORM boilerplate that `DeriveEntityModel` relies on.
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}

impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

Key facts:

  • DeriveEntityModel is the Sea-ORM half. It owns the #[sea_orm(...)] namespace, generates the Entity, Column, PrimaryKey, Relation, and ActiveModel types, and is required on every FerraModel struct.
  • FerraModel is the Ferra half. It reads #[sea_orm(primary_key)] and #[sea_orm(table_name)], plus the #[ferra(...)] namespace, and emits a static ModelMeta that every downstream Ferra crate reads.
  • Serialize + Deserialize are required by the FerraModel supertrait bound. ferra-forge does not auto-inject them — see the next section.
  • Visibility must be at least pub(crate). Private structs trip class 8 (FRG-008) of the Troubleshooting table.

Recognised field types:

Rust typeFieldType variantNotes
StringStringUTF-8 string.
i32I3232-bit signed integer.
i64I6464-bit signed integer.
f64F6464-bit IEEE-754 float.
boolBoolBoolean.
Uuid (or ferra::Id)UuidUUID, always present.
Option<String>OptionStringNullable string.
Option<i32>OptionI32Nullable 32-bit integer.
Option<i64>OptionI64Nullable 64-bit integer.
Option<f64>OptionF64Nullable float.
Option<bool>OptionBoolNullable boolean.
Option<Uuid> (or Option<Id>)OptionUuidNullable UUID. Surfaces in OpenAPI as "type": ["string","null"] with "format": "uuid" (the OpenAPI 3.1 nullable form). Cannot be combined with #[sea_orm(primary_key)] — that contradiction emits FRG-215.
ferra::DateTime, ferra::Date, ferra::Time (and Option<..>)Timestamp, Date, Time (Option..)Ferra’s time vocabulary; chrono, time and jiff types are refused. See ferra-core.md § Time vocabulary.
serde_json::Value (or Json), Option<..> of them; any serde type with #[field(json)]Json, OptionJsonA JSON document, bounded in depth and size (json(max_depth = .., max_bytes = ..)), never filterable, sortable or a cursor key (FRG-355). See ferra-core.md § JSON documents.

Relations

A model written with #[sea_orm::model] (Sea-ORM’s dense form) may declare its relations inline, as HasMany<..>, HasOne<..> or BelongsTo<..> fields. The macro expands the struct twice: Model keeps the scalar fields, a second struct ModelEx keeps all of them. #[derive(FerraModel)] runs on both. On Model it reads the columns as ever, so a relation field is never a column, a wire field or a projection field. On ModelEx it emits the relation metadata and nothing else.

use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod client {
    use super::*;

    #[sea_orm::model]
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "clients")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub name: String,
        #[sea_orm(has_many)]
        pub contexts: HasMany<super::context::Entity>,
    }

    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

mod context {
    use super::*;

    #[sea_orm::model]
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "contexts")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub client_id: i32,
        #[sea_orm(belongs_to, from = "client_id", to = "id")]
        pub client: BelongsTo<super::client::Entity>,
    }

    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
fn main() {}

A relation field is only valid in this form. On a struct that is not an expansion of #[sea_orm::model], such as a hand-written Model with an enum Relation, it is refused (FRG-125, see ferra-forge-diagnostics.md). The split form stays valid for a model without relation fields.

Explicit serde derives are required

ferra-forge does not add #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)] for you. If you omit them, rustc fires E0277 with the span pinned to your struct’s name:

error[E0277]: the trait bound `Model: serde::Serialize` is not satisfied
  --> src/my_module.rs:7:12
   |
 7 | pub struct Model {
   |            ^^^^^ unsatisfied trait bound
   |
   = note: for local types consider adding `#[derive(serde::Serialize)]` to your `Model` type
note: required by a bound in `_assert_ferra_model_bounds`

The fix is always the same: add #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)] to the derive list.

Why not auto-inject? A user with use serde::Serialize as S; #[derive(S)] would trip a naive name-based detector into silent double-derive and hit E0119 conflicting-impls. Delegating to the trait-bound solver is correct by construction.

Three attribute namespaces, two policies

ferra-forge reads three attribute namespaces with deliberately different handling:

NamespaceOwnerPurposeUnknown-key policy
#[sea_orm(...)]Sea-ORMPersistence shape (table name, primary key, column type)silently ignored by ferra-forge
#[ferra(...)]FerraExposure flags (read_only, write_only, skip, resource)hard compile_error!
#[field(...)]FerraDeclarative validation rules (min_length, email, …) — see § Validation rules; query markers (filterable, sortable, cursor_key, pagination.md); owner; json, json(max_depth = .., max_bytes = .., schema = ..) for a JSON document (ferra-core.md § JSON documents)hard compile_error! (FRG-213)

The asymmetry is load-bearing. Consider the worked example:

// Security-critical typo. The user MEANT `write_only`.
#[ferra(writeonly)]
pub password_hash: String,

(The complete model of this typo, bad and good, compiled, is FRG-308.)

Because #[ferra(writeonly)] is not recognised, the build fails:

error: FRG-308: `#[ferra(writeonly)]` is not a recognized attribute
         help: did you mean `write_only`?
         note: see docs/user-guide/ferra-forge-diagnostics.md § FRG-308
  --> src/models/user.rs:12:13
   |
12 |     #[ferra(writeonly)]
   |             ^^^^^^^^^

If Ferra had accepted the typo, password_hash would quietly serialise into API responses — a Broken Object Property Level Authorization (OWASP API Top 10 #3). The hard-fail rule makes this class of bug unshippable.

Conversely, an unknown-to-Ferra but Sea-ORM-permitted key such as #[sea_orm(rename_all = "camelCase")] passes through Ferra silently — it is Sea-ORM’s concern, not Ferra’s, and pre-validating it inside ferra-forge would saddle Ferra with every Sea-ORM minor-release vocabulary change.

Where each namespace goes

The derive reads each namespace in one place only. An attribute written somewhere else used to compile and do nothing, which for a security declaration is the worst outcome; from 0.14.0 it is refused with FRG-138, spanned on the attribute path.

AttributeOn the structOn a field
#[ferra(...)]container keys (auth, resource, projection(...), system_only, …)field flags (read_only, write_only, skip, computed)
#[field(...)]refused, FRG-138validation rules, query markers, owner, read, write
#[authorize(...)]the model’s rulesrefused, FRG-138: a field’s rule is #[field(read = …, write = …)]
#[behavior(...)]the behaviorsrefused, FRG-138
#[operation(...)]refused, FRG-335refused, FRG-138

On a relation field of the dense #[sea_orm::model] form, every Ferra attribute above is refused with FRG-122 instead.

Field names on the wire

The JSON name of a field is its Rust name (release_year) unless the model says otherwise. One declaration switches every field of the model to camelCase:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "bearer", rename_all = "camelCase")]
#[ferra(projection(name = "summary", read = [id, film_title], write = [film_title]))]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    #[field(filterable, sortable)]
    pub film_title: String,
    #[field(filterable, sortable)]
    pub release_year: i64,
    #[field(owner)]
    pub owner_id: Uuid,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
POST /films                      {"filmTitle": "Arrival", "releaseYear": 2016}
201                              {"id": 1, "filmTitle": "Arrival", "releaseYear": 2016,
                                  "ownerId": "0190a4a0-…", "_links": {…}}
GET  /films?filter[releaseYear]=2016&sort=-filmTitle
GET  /summary/films/1            {"id": 1, "filmTitle": "Arrival", "_links": {…}}

That is the only thing to write. Do not add #[serde(rename_all = ...)]: Ferra translates the names itself, in both directions, and a serde rename does not compile (FRG-116, below).

Where each name is used

The wire name (releaseYear)The Rust name (release_year)
request bodies and responses, on the bare path and under every projectionthe struct field
filter[releaseYear]=… and sort=releaseYear / sort=-releaseYearread = [...] and write = [...] lists of a projection
field names in 400 and 422 answers#[field(...)] and #[ferra(...)] markers
the OpenAPI document: properties, required, parameters, examplesthe SQL column (rename the column with #[sea_orm(column_name = "...")])

Rules

  • Accepted values: "camelCase" and "snake_case" (the default — same as no attribute). Any other value does not compile (FRG-325). There is no per-field rename in 0.9.0.

  • The Rust names are not names of the API any more: a body key release_year is refused with 422 (unknown field), filter[release_year] and sort=release_year with 400 — the answer lists the accepted names.

  • The conversion is serde’s camelCase rule: each _ is dropped and the next character upper-cased; the first character is lower-cased.

    RustJSON
    release_yearreleaseYear
    owner_idownerId
    line_2line2
    a__baB
    _privateprivate
    r#typetype

  • Two fields must not end up with the same JSON name (line_2 and line2), and no field may be named _links on the wire — the key Ferra adds to every response object. Both are compile errors (FRG-326).

What is not renamed

  • URL paths and the resource name (/films, /summary/films/1).
  • The keys Ferra adds around your fields: items, page, per_page, total, next_cursor, _links; the query parameters page, per_page, cursor, sort, filter[...]; the members of an error body (type, title, status, detail, errors).
  • What your own code serializes. The translation is done by the routes Ferra generates. A handler of yours that returns the Model serializes it with serde: Rust names, and every field. Answer with a struct of your own in that handler.

serde attributes on a model

A serde attribute that changes a field’s JSON name, presence or text would bypass the translation above, so it does not compile (FRG-116):

WhereRefusedAllowed
on a fieldrename, alias, flatten, skip, skip_serializing, skip_deserializing, skip_serializing_if, serialize_with, deserialize_with, with, getterdefault, borrow, bound
on the modelrename_all, rename_all_fields, tag, transparent, from, try_from, into, remoterename (the type’s name), default, bound, deny_unknown_fields, crate, expecting

A #[serde(...)] attribute Ferra cannot read is refused too. To keep a field out of the API, use Ferra’s own markers: #[ferra(skip)] (never in the API), #[ferra(read_only)] (never written by a client) or #[ferra(write_only)] (never returned). #[sea_orm(rename_all = "...")] is unrelated: it names SQL columns.

Recognised #[ferra(...)] keys

Container-level

KeyValueSemantics
resourcenon-empty string literalOverride the default resource_name in the emitted ModelMeta.
rename_all"camelCase" or "snake_case"JSON names of the model’s fields. Default "snake_case" (the Rust names). See § Field names on the wire.
client_pkflagThe client supplies the primary key in the create body (composite or natural keys). Without it the server chooses the key.
authorityflagThe application decides access with its own code: impl FerraAuthority (and FerraListAuthority) for the model, and Model::FIELDS to build conditions. See ferra-auth.md § Programmatic authority.

The default resource_name is the #[sea_orm(table_name)] literal if present, otherwise snake_case(<StructIdent>) with a simple English plural suffix (Film → films, UserProfile → user_profiles, Category → categories, Box → boxes). The {Model} of the OpenAPI schema names (Film, FilmSummary) is the singular of this resource name, not the struct ident, which is Model in every Sea-ORM entity.

Declarative behaviors (#[behavior(soft_delete)], #[behavior(timestampable)], and the cross-cutting cohort surface they share) are documented separately in behaviors.md. Enrolling a model in a behavior is a container-level act — declaring the behavior on the struct opts every operation on that model into the cohort’s contract.

Field-level

Flagreadablewritableskip_api
(none)truetruefalse
#[ferra(read_only)]truefalsefalse
#[ferra(write_only)]falsetruefalse
#[ferra(skip)]falsefalsetrue

#[ferra(read_only)] and #[ferra(write_only)] on the same field contradict — see FRG-302. #[ferra(write_only)] on a primary-key field contradicts the id’s always-readable invariant — see FRG-304. Repeated identical flags are idempotent.

#[ferra(write_only)] is structurally excluded from every read

#[ferra(write_only)] is the framework’s load-bearing primitive for fields that must be inbound-accepting but never outbound-leaking — canonically a password hash, an API-key plaintext, or any other write-side credential.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize, Clone, Debug, PartialEq)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "users")]
#[ferra(auth = "bearer")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub email: String,
    #[ferra(write_only)]
    pub password_hash: String,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

What the framework guarantees:

  • POST /users and PUT /users/{id} accept password_hash in the request body, validate it, and persist it through the standard insert / update pipeline.
  • Every read response — single-item GET /users/{id}, collection GET /users, and the create / update response envelopes — omits password_hash. There is no header, query parameter, or Accept: variant that flips the field on.
  • The same exclusion applies to every named projection: the auto-derived {Model}{Projection}ReadProjection struct emitted by ferra-forge does not have the field as a member, so the type system itself blocks any future handler from re-introducing it.

Structural-by-construction, not runtime-filter

The ferra-forge proc-macro emits one pub struct {Model}ReadProjection per model, whose field list does not contain any #[ferra(write_only)] field. Two things keep the field out of a response:

  • the generated routes serialise the model to a JSON value and keep only the keys of the route’s read projection (projection.rs), so the field is dropped at run time, before the JSON leaves the framework;
  • the resource access (Resource<M>) returns <M as FerraViews>::Read, the struct above, which has no such member: a hand-written route that answers with it cannot leak password_hash, because the field does not exist on the type the response carries.

Prior to 0.6.5 the exclusion lived only in the OpenAPI emitter and a runtime serialiser filter; the 0.6.5 promotion to a structural guarantee closes the OWASP API #3 mitigation gap.

Generated items: the views of a model

Next to the projection structs, #[derive(FerraModel)] emits what the resource access speaks (FerraViews, ADR-0058):

  • {Model}Patch: one Option<T> per field of the bare route’s write projection (write-only fields included, the key, the owner and read-only fields not). A nullable field is Option<Option<T>>: None leaves the column, Some(None) writes null. An unset entry is left out when the patch is serialized (RFC 7396).
  • impl From<{Model}> for {Model}ReadProjection, and for every named read projection: a field-by-field move. On a #[behavior(timestampable)] model the two stamps are Option<DateTime> members the projection lists, None here: the model does not carry the columns.
  • impl FerraViews for {Model}: Read, Write and Patch name the structs the bare route serves, or those of the projection promoted with default = true; Ferra puts the stamps of a row into Read.

There is no “opt-in” — FRG-305 rejects the obvious workaround

Listing a #[ferra(write_only)] field in any projection’s read = [...] is rejected at compile time with diagnostic FRG-305:

error: FRG-305: projection `admin` lists field `password_hash` in `read`, but the field is declared `#[ferra(write_only)]`
         help: remove the ident from `read = [...]`, or remove `#[ferra(write_only)]` from the field declaration
         note: the write-only declaration is enforced by construction — a write-only field cannot appear in any read projection's struct; see docs/user-guide/ferra-forge-diagnostics.md § FRG-305
  --> src/models/user.rs:16:55
   |
16 | #[ferra(projection(name = "admin", read = [id, email, password_hash]))]
   |                                                       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^

If you genuinely need the field to appear in some read surface, the resolution is to drop #[ferra(write_only)] from the field declaration entirely. The field then appears in every read by default; use #[ferra(skip)] or a per-projection read = [...] allowlist to scope the surfaces that include it. See projections-and-routing.md for the projection key set and the auto-derived URL prefix contract.

The full FRG-3NN diagnostic family for write-only-related mistakes (FRG-302 through FRG-307, FRG-314) is documented in ferra-forge-diagnostics.md.

Computed fields

A computed field is server-derived: the framework runs the developer’s compute function after every fetch and before serialisation, then carries the produced value out through the read response. The field is excluded from INSERT / UPDATE SQL and from every write projection’s struct, so a request body that carries it is refused (422: the field is not one the client may write) — the only path to set the field is the compute hook the developer writes.

The #[ferra(computed)] attribute

Tag the field with #[ferra(computed)] and write an impl FerraComputed for {Model} block that overrides the method matching your computation kind:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use ferra::compute::FerraComputed;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "invoices")]
#[ferra(auth = "bearer")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub subtotal: f64,
    pub tax: f64,
    #[sea_orm(ignore)]
    #[ferra(computed)]
    pub total: f64,
}

impl FerraComputed for Model {
    fn compute(&mut self) {
        self.total = self.subtotal + self.tax;
    }
}

#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}

impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

#[ferra(computed)] implies writable = false and read_only = true. The framework injects a ferra_core::diagnostics::FerraComputedDefault bound on the field’s type — see the Compile-time rejections sub-section below for the consequence when that bound fails.

The three tiers

FerraComputed exposes three default-implemented methods covering the spectrum from pure derivations to N+1-eliminating batched I/O. An implementer overrides only the method matching the computation kind.

  • fn compute(&mut self) — synchronous, zero I/O. The right choice for total = subtotal + tax and other in-row derivations. Cost shape: one function call per row, no async overhead. Default: no-op.
  • fn compute_async(&mut self, ctx: &RequestContext) — per-row async with a request-context handle. The right choice for per-row I/O (currency-rate lookup, external HTTP enrichment). Cost shape: one I/O round-trip per row — invoke this tier only when the computation genuinely cannot be batched.
