FRG-400 — two copies of Sea-ORM

Trigger. The application declares sea-orm in its own [dependencies], and cargo resolved that declaration and the one of ferra to different versions: the build holds two copies of the crate. Ferra’s routes read and write through ferra::sea_orm; every Sea-ORM type the application names is then a different type from the one Ferra expects. Without this code the compiler words it as “expected DatabaseConnection, found DatabaseConnection”, far from the cause. #[derive(FerraModel)] checks it, at the model, wherever the application’s sea-orm is there next to ferra, under the condition of the dependency itself:

  • sea-orm in [dependencies]: in every build;
  • sea-orm with optional = true: in the builds where one of the features that enable it is on (#[cfg(feature = "…")]: the implicit feature named like the dependency, or the features that write "dep:sea-orm" or "sea-orm/…");
  • sea-orm under [target.'cfg(…)'.dependencies]: where that cfg(…) holds;
  • sea-orm in [dev-dependencies]: under #[cfg(test)], which is the crate’s unit tests, integration tests (tests/) and benches. An example (examples/) has the dev-dependency too but nothing in the code tells it apart from the ordinary build, so there two copies show as the compiler’s own “expected DatabaseConnection, found DatabaseConnection”;
  • sea-orm under [target.<triple>.dependencies], named by a target triple and not by a cfg(…): no check, for the same reason.

Where the application’s copy is not there, the derive reaches Sea-ORM through ferra::sea_orm, and there is one copy to compare. A model with projections may add type errors of its own after FRG-400 under such a condition.

The rule: a Ferra project never holds two major versions of Sea-ORM, not even for its tests or an optional feature. The check is armed by the condition of the dependency, so a sea-orm = "1" that is only a dev-dependency, or only behind a feature (full = ["dep:sea-orm"]), is refused as soon as that condition holds (cargo test, --features full), next to a model written through the facade (use ferra::prelude::*;). Before 0.9.0 this compiled by accident; it is refused on purpose, because the model and Ferra’s routes would then speak of two different DatabaseConnections whenever the test or the feature is on. A declaration that is never active (a cfg(any()) table, an optional dependency no feature enables) is not a copy and is not refused. The remedy is the one below: give that sea-orm Ferra’s major, or remove it; cargo tree -d -i sea-orm (add --all-features for an optional one) lists the copies.

error[E0277]: FRG-400: the `sea-orm` your application declares is not the `sea-orm` Ferra was built with (`DatabaseConnection` is not `DatabaseConnection`)
   |         Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize,
   |                                                         ^^^^^^^^^^ this model is written against another copy of `sea-orm` than the one Ferra's routes use

Bad.

[dependencies]
ferra   = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.13.1" } # built with sea-orm 2.x
sea-orm = "1"                                                           # another major

Good.

[dependencies]
ferra   = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.13.1" }
sea-orm = { version = "2.0", default-features = false, features = ["macros", "runtime-tokio-rustls", "sqlx-postgres"] }

Fix. Give sea-orm the same major version as Ferra, in [dependencies], [dev-dependencies] and under every feature (the CHANGELOG.md of each release says which), then check that one copy is left: cargo tree -d -i sea-orm prints nothing when it is. Or declare no sea-orm at all and write ferra::sea_orm::… (put use ferra::prelude::*; or use ferra::sea_orm; at the top of each file that uses a Sea-ORM derive). sea-orm-migration, if the project has migrations, follows the same major.

Fixture. crates/ferra-forge/tests/ui/fail_two_sea_orm_copies.rs pins the message. A second copy of a crate cannot be built inside a fixture, so it uses two stand-in types; that the derive emits the bound, and that it holds when there is one copy, is shown by crates/ferra/tests/sea_orm_direct_style.rs.

Custom handlers

Most Ferra apps need at least one route that is not pure CRUD — a publish action, a derived collection, an aggregation, a webhook receiver. This page is the authoritative guide to writing those handlers on top of a Ferra-served API. A reader with this page plus standard Rust knowledge produces a compiling action route on the first attempt — no framework source, no ADR, no constitution required.

The companion CRUD / envelope / Tower-stack / typed-extraction reference is ferra-http.md. The router-assembly facade is foundry.md.

Dependencies. The examples on this page assume the dependencies of Getting started:

[dependencies]
ferra   = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.13.1" }
sea-orm = { version = "2.0", default-features = false, features = ["macros", "runtime-tokio-rustls", "sqlx-postgres"] }
tokio   = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread"] }
axum    = "0.8"
serde   = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }

When the generated routes are not enough

The five built-in handlers cover the resource-shaped endpoints — list, read, create, update, delete. They are all you need for ~80 % of the surface a typical app exposes.

You write a custom handler when the route is not one of those five operations. Common reasons:

  • Action routes. POST /films/{id}/publish, POST /invoices/{id}/cancel, POST /accounts/{id}/transfer — verbs on a resource that aren’t expressible as PUT.
  • Derived collections. GET /films/popular, GET /actors/{id}/films — collections whose membership is computed, not just SELECT * WHERE ....
  • Multi-resource projections. GET /dashboard returning a join of three resources at once.
  • Webhook receivers. POST /webhooks/stripe reading a non-Ferra payload shape.
  • Cross-cutting endpoints. GET /healthz, GET /metrics.

Custom handlers are plain Axum handlers. They accept Axum extractors, return Result<_, FerraError> for RFC 7807 error continuity, and compose with the framework router by appending .route(...) or .merge(...) on the value Foundry::build() returns.

The worked example: POST /films/{id}/publish

The complete shape of an action route — model declaration, handler signature, composition with Foundry — in one file. The route reaches the films table through Resource<Film>: it is judged by the rules of PUT /films/{id}, not by whatever the handler remembers to check. Drop this into a fresh src/main.rs whose Cargo.toml declares the canonical dependency set (ferra, tokio, serde, sea-orm as in Getting Started, and axum with its macros feature, which #[axum::debug_handler] needs) and it compiles.

use axum::{Json, Router, routing::post};
use ferra::{
    ClaimCheck, Date, FerraError, FerraIdentity, FerraJson, FerraModel, FerraPath, Foundry,
    HmacAlgorithm, JwtConfig, Resource, ResourceHandle,
};
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

// --- The model -----------------------------------------------------

mod film {
    use super::*;

    #[derive(
        Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq,
        DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel,
        Serialize, Deserialize,
    )]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "bearer")] // the posture every model declares; see ferra-auth.md
    #[authorize(              // a film belongs to the caller who created it
        list = IsOwner,
        get = IsOwner,
        create = Authenticated,
        update = IsOwner,
        delete = IsOwner
    )]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        #[sea_orm(unique)]
        pub title: String,
        pub director: String,
        pub year: Option<i32>,
        pub release_date: Option<Date>,
        pub published: bool,
        #[field(owner)]
        pub owner_id: Uuid,
    }

    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}

    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

pub use film::Model as Film;

// --- Who the caller is ---------------------------------------------

#[derive(Clone, Debug, Deserialize)]
struct Claims {
    sub: String,
}

impl FerraIdentity for Claims {
    fn id(&self) -> &str {
        &self.sub
    }
    fn has_role(&self, _role: &str) -> bool {
        false
    }
}

// --- The action's request body -------------------------------------

// Plain serde struct — nothing Ferra-specific. The `FerraJson<T>`
// extractor on the handler signature accepts any `T: DeserializeOwned`.
#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct PublishRequest {
    release_date: Option<Date>,
}

// --- The action's response body ------------------------------------

// A route of your own answers with a body of its own: the fields you
// choose, under the names you choose.
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct PublishedFilm {
    id: i32,
    title: String,
    published: bool,
    release_date: Option<Date>,
}

// --- The handler ---------------------------------------------------

// `#[axum::debug_handler]` is optional but turns the dense
// `Handler` trait-bound error into a single, targeted message
// when one of the rules below is violated. Keep it on while
// iterating; it is a no-op at runtime.
#[axum::debug_handler(state = ResourceHandle<Film>)]
async fn publish_film(
    // FromRequestParts — binds the caller (the bearer token) and gives
    //                   access to the films, under the films' rules.
    films: Resource<Film>,
    // FromRequestParts — `FerraPath` is the typed-extraction
    //                   wrapper around `axum::extract::Path<T>`.
    FerraPath(id): FerraPath<i32>,
    // FromRequest — `FerraJson` consumes the request body. Body-
    //              consuming extractors MUST be the LAST argument.
    FerraJson(body): FerraJson<PublishRequest>,
) -> Result<Json<PublishedFilm>, FerraError> {
    // Same rules as `PUT /films/{id}`: another caller's film is a 404 and
    // the row is unchanged. Only `published` and `release_date` are written.
    let patch = film::ModelPatch {
        published: Some(true),
        release_date: body.release_date.map(Some),
        ..Default::default()
    };
    let film = films.update(id, patch).await?;

    // Answer with the fields this action exposes.
    Ok(Json(PublishedFilm {
        id: film.id,
        title: film.title,
        published: film.published,
        release_date: film.release_date,
    }))
}

// --- Composition with Foundry --------------------------------------

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let database_url = std::env::var("DATABASE_URL")?;
    let conn = sea_orm::Database::connect(&database_url).await?;

    let jwt = JwtConfig::single_secret(
        "key-1",
        std::env::var("JWT_SECRET")?,
        HmacAlgorithm::Hs256,
        ClaimCheck::expect("https://auth.example.com/"),
        ClaimCheck::expect("films-api"),
    )?;

    // `mount_and_handle` mounts `Film` as `.mount::<Film>()` does — the CRUD
    // routes, the JWT layer — and returns the handle that routes of your own
    // use to reach the films.
    let (foundry, films) = Foundry::new(conn)
        .with_auth::<Claims>(jwt)
        .mount_and_handle::<Film>();
    let api = foundry.with_docs().build();

    // The action route lives on a sibling sub-router whose state is the
    // handle. `ResourceHandle<M>: Clone` (reference counts only).
    let custom = Router::new()
        .route("/films/{id}/publish", post(publish_film))
        .with_state(films);

    let app = api.merge(custom);

    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:3000").await?;
    // The rate limiter keys on the peer address: serve with connect info.
    axum::serve(listener, app.into_make_service_with_connect_info::<std::net::SocketAddr>()).await?;
    Ok(())
}

film::ModelPatch is the struct #[derive(FerraModel)] generates next to Model ({Model}Patch, one Option<T> per writable field, None leaving the column; also <Film as FerraViews>::Patch). The owner column is compared with the token’s sub rendered as a string, so a Uuid owner_id matches a sub holding that UUID (ferra-auth.md).

Resource<Film> has six methods — get, list, list_cursor, create, update, delete — each of which does what the generated route of the same name does: it runs the authorization checkpoint of the operation, scopes a list to the caller’s rows under IsOwner, stamps the owner on create, validates with the model’s #[field(...)] rules, and writes under the owner’s guard. What it hands back is the model’s read view, <Film as FerraViews>::Read: a #[ferra(write_only)] column is not a member of that type, so a route cannot send it by mistake. ferra-http.md is the reference.

Field rules reach a route of your own (0.13.0). A field with a #[field(read = …, write = …)] rule is judged for the bound caller by Resource<M> as it is by the generated routes. What get, list and list_cursor return has each field the caller may not read set to None, so a route that serializes it sends no such key (never null); an IsOwner read rule is judged row by row. A gated field of the write view, and of a patch, is an Option (Option<Option<T>> when the column is nullable): None is left alone, Some(None) is null, and a field the caller may not read or write that you set is refused like the generated route refuses it (422, then 403), the row unchanged. A filter on a field the caller may not read is refused as on the route, and a sort on it keeps the default order.

Hooks (0.13.0). Resource<M>::create and Resource<M>::update run the model’s before_save and after_save hooks, and Resource<M>::delete its before_delete and after_delete, in the write’s transaction, as the generated routes do (Hooks).

No response envelope in 0.9.0. The routes Foundry generates answer with the row filtered through its read projection, under its wire names, flat or with HAL _links as the client’s Accept chooses. That envelope is not public: a route of your own would build links that know neither the base path, nor the version prefix, nor the configured origin. Answer with a struct of your own, as above. The same goes for #[ferra(rename_all = "camelCase")]: the read view carries the model’s Rust field names, so a route that serializes it sends those, not the wire names of the generated routes.

A successful POST /films/42/publish with body {"release_date": "2026-05-10"} returns 200 OK:

{
  "id": 42,
  "title": "Rust en pratique",
  "published": true,
  "release_date": "2026-05-10"
}

Errors flow through the same FerraError taxonomy the built-in handlers use — a malformed JSON body returns 400 with type: "https://ferra.rs/errors/validation"; a film that is not yours returns 404 with type: "https://ferra.rs/errors/not_found", the same answer as a film that does not exist; no token is a 401. Clients that handle one Ferra error already handle this one.

Extractor ordering: FromRequest vs FromRequestParts

Axum has two extractor traits. The distinction looks academic until you write your first multi-extractor handler — then it becomes the load-bearing rule.

TraitReads fromExamplesPosition
FromRequestPartsrequest parts only (method, URI, headers, state)State<T>, Path<T>, Query<T>, Parts, HeaderMap, FerraPath<T>any position
FromRequestthe whole request, including the body (consumed)Json<T>, Bytes, String, Form<T>, FerraJson<T>last argument only

The rule: at most one body-consuming extractor (FromRequest) per handler, and it MUST be the last argument. Every other extractor is body-agnostic (FromRequestParts) and goes earlier.

This is a fundamental property of HTTP, not an Axum design quirk: a request body is a one-shot stream. Once you have read it, the bytes are gone.

The handler in the worked example follows the rule:

async fn publish_film(
    films: Resource<Film>,                    // FromRequestParts
    FerraPath(id): FerraPath<i32>,            // FromRequestParts
    FerraJson(body): FerraJson<PublishRequest>, // FromRequest — LAST
) -> Result<...> { ... }

(An excerpt of the handler above, which is the compiled version.)

Reorder FerraJson ahead of FerraPath and the build fails. Without #[axum::debug_handler] the compiler reports the violation through a deep trait-bound chain on Handler. With #[axum::debug_handler] the diagnostic points directly at the offending argument.

Multiple body extractors. Axum allows exactly one body-consuming extractor per handler. If you legitimately need to look at the raw bytes and a typed JSON deserialization, do both inside a single FromRequest-implementing wrapper, or read Bytes and parse it explicitly with serde_json::from_slice. There is no Json<A> + Json<B> shape.

Send + Sync + 'static: the bound-set cheat-sheet

Tokio runs handlers on a multi-threaded executor by default. Every value Axum carries through the handler must be sendable across threads and outlive the request. The compiler enforces this through Send + Sync + 'static-shaped bounds on the Handler trait — failures here look daunting at first read.

The cheat-sheet:

SymptomLikely causeFix
the trait Send is not implemented for ... inside an async fna !Send value is held across an .await (Rc<_>, RefCell<_>, MutexGuard from std::sync::Mutex)use Arc<_>, tokio::sync::Mutex, or restructure so the offending value is dropped before the .await
the trait Sync is not implemented for ... on State<T>the state type is not Sync (e.g., it owns a non-Sync cache)wrap the inner shared state in Arc<RwLock<...>> or restructure to a channel
argument requires that ... must outlive 'staticthe handler captures a non-'static reference (&str from outside the closure, a borrow from the request)own the data (String, Bytes), or extract it via an extractor
Handler<_, _> not satisfied with a long, hard-to-read chainusually one of the three above, hidden behind Handler’s blanket impladd #[axum::debug_handler] and read the first targeted error it produces

Notes on the framework’s own types:

  • ResourceHandle<M> is Clone + Send + Sync + 'static — it wraps a shared connection. Keep it in the router state and pass it through any number of handlers freely.
  • FerraJson<T> / FerraPath<T> add no bounds beyond the inner T: DeserializeOwned + Send + 'static that Axum already requires.
  • FerraError is Send + Sync + 'static and implements axum::response::IntoResponse — return Result<_, FerraError> from any handler signature.

If your handler async fn body holds a !Send value across an .await, the bound failure surfaces in the Handler impl, not in the body. Move the value into a synchronous block or drop it before the await.

Friendlier diagnostics with #[axum::debug_handler]

Axum’s Handler trait has a blanket impl that erases per-argument type information by the time the bound failure is reported. Without help, a single wrong extractor produces a multi-screen not satisfied chain.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use axum::Json;
use ferra::{FerraError, FerraPath};

#[axum::debug_handler]
async fn my_handler(FerraPath(id): FerraPath<i32>) -> Result<Json<i32>, FerraError> {
    Ok(Json(id))
}
}

The proc-macro re-checks the arguments one by one and emits a single targeted error per offending argument:

  • Json must be the last extractor
  • the trait FromRequestParts is not implemented for …
  • Send is not satisfied because …

It is purely a development aid — it adds no runtime cost and emits no code in release builds. Keep it on every custom handler while iterating; remove it only if a transitive dep needs the un-decorated handler signature for some other proc-macro to see.

It does not (and cannot) flag every misuse — extractor ordering and bound failures are visible to it; subtle data-flow bugs and panic-on-unwrap paths are not.

FerraJson<T> and FerraPath<T> — RFC 7807 error continuity

Axum’s stock Json<T> and Path<T> produce text/plain 400 bodies on rejection. A consumer that handles Ferra’s application/problem+json taxonomy elsewhere on the API gets a mixed wire format on the rejection path — two parsers, two error shapes, two test surfaces.

FerraJson<T> and FerraPath<T> are thin newtypes around the stock extractors that intercept the rejection and remap it to FerraError::Validation:

pub struct FerraJson<T>(pub T);   // wraps axum::Json<T>
pub struct FerraPath<T>(pub T);   // wraps axum::extract::Path<T>

The output on a malformed body looks like every other Ferra 400:

{
  "type":   "https://ferra.rs/errors/validation",
  "title":  "Validation Error",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "validation failed",
  "errors": [
    { "field": "body", "code": "invalid_json",
      "message": "expected `,` or `}` at line 1 column 14" }
  ]
}

Use the wrappers in every custom handler that takes JSON or path parameters. The single-token swap from Json<T> → FerraJson<T> and Path<T> → FerraPath<T> is the only difference.

What if I genuinely want stock Axum extraction? You can — they coexist. A handler that takes axum::Json<T> produces stock 400 text/plain on rejection; one that takes FerraJson<T> produces RFC 7807. Pick per handler.

errors[*].code is drawn from the closed list in ferra-error-handling.md § Validation codes; these wrappers produce invalid_json and invalid_path_param. New codes are additive — existing consumer branches keep matching.

Composing with Foundry

Two composition patterns, in order of how often you reach for them:

1. Append routes on top of Foundry::build()

use axum::{Router, routing::post};
use ferra::Foundry;
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
        pub published: bool,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
async fn publish_film() {}
fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection) {
let (builder, films) = Foundry::new(conn).mount_and_handle::<Film>();
let api = builder.with_docs().build();

let custom = Router::new()
    .route("/films/{id}/publish", post(publish_film))
    .with_state(films);

let app: Router = api.merge(custom);
let _ = app;
}
fn main() {}

The framework’s Tower stack (CORS, body-limit, tracing, rate-limit on mutation routes) wraps every Ferra-mounted resource. Routes you append on the outer Router see the framework’s outer layers but not the per-resource inner layers — your action endpoint does NOT inherit the rate-limit layer that mounts on the CRUD mutation sub-router. Add your own where needed.

2. Hand-rolled Router with no Ferra CRUD at all

use axum::{Router, routing::{get, post}};
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
        pub published: bool,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
async fn publish_film() {}
fn demo() {
let app: Router = Router::new()
    .route("/healthz", get(|| async { "ok" }))
    .route("/films/{id}/publish", post(publish_film));
let _ = app;
}
fn main() {}

For apps that are only action routes, with no CRUD surface to derive (and so no model to reach: your own state, if the routes need one, is yours). You retain FerraJson / FerraPath / FerraError; you give up the auto-generated CRUD, the HAL _links on the responses, and the docs surface.

In both patterns, consumer-added .layer(...) calls on the final Router wrap the framework stack from the outside. Place observability and authentication layers there; place per-route policy where the policy belongs (a sub-router scoped to that route).

A route you add yourself is outside Ferra’s authorization policy: Foundry protects the routes it mounts, not yours. Protect a custom route yourself, for instance with the CurrentUser<YourClaims> extractor behind the JWT layer (see ferra-auth.md).

use std::sync::Arc;
use axum::{Router, http::StatusCode, middleware::from_fn_with_state, routing::post};
use ferra::{CurrentUser, FerraAuthLayer, FerraError, FerraIdentity, Foundry, JwtConfig};
use ferra::ferra_auth_enforcing_middleware;
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
        pub published: bool,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Deserialize)]
struct YourClaims { sub: String }
impl FerraIdentity for YourClaims {
    fn id(&self) -> &str { &self.sub }
    fn has_role(&self, _role: &str) -> bool { false }
}

// `CurrentUser` rejects with 401 when the request carries no identity.
async fn publish_film(
    CurrentUser(user): CurrentUser<YourClaims>,
    /* other extractors */
) -> Result<StatusCode, FerraError> {
    // check `user` against your own rule here, return FerraError::Forbidden to refuse
    let _ = user;
    Ok(StatusCode::NO_CONTENT)
}

fn demo(conn: sea_orm::DatabaseConnection, jwt_config: JwtConfig) {
let jwt = Arc::new(jwt_config); // the same `JwtConfig` settings you give `.with_auth`
let (_api, films) = Foundry::new(conn).mount_and_handle::<Film>();
let custom: Router = Router::new()
    .route("/films/{id}/publish", post(publish_film))
    .with_state(films)
    .layer(from_fn_with_state(
        FerraAuthLayer::<YourClaims>::new(jwt),
        ferra_auth_enforcing_middleware::<YourClaims>,
    ));
let _ = custom;
}
fn main() {}

To unit-test such a handler, call it with CurrentUser(claims) — the tuple field is public, no token is needed. To test it behind the layer, sign a token with ferra::testing::bearer (see ferra-auth.md § Testing authenticated routes).

Raw database access, outside the contract

Ferra hands out no repository: ResourceHandle<M> and Resource<M> are the only way to a model’s rows through Ferra, and they apply the generated routes’ rules. A query they do not cover (a join, an aggregate, a report) is yours to write against your own DatabaseConnection. That connection is not Ferra’s: nothing checks the caller, scopes the owner or filters soft-deleted rows for you, and it is outside Ferra’s stability contract.

Keep both in one state and let Axum derive each part:

use axum::{Json, Router, extract::{FromRef, State}, http::StatusCode, routing::get};
use ferra::{DatabaseConnection, Foundry, ResourceHandle};
use sea_orm::{EntityTrait, PaginatorTrait};
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
mod film {
    use super::*;
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
    #[ferra(auth = "none")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub title: String,
        pub published: bool,
    }
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
    pub enum Relation {}
    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
use film::Model as Film;

#[derive(Clone, FromRef)]
struct AppState {
    films: ResourceHandle<Film>, // `Resource<Film>` is extracted from it
    conn: DatabaseConnection,    // yours: raw queries, no checkpoint
}

async fn count_films(State(conn): State<DatabaseConnection>) -> Result<Json<u64>, StatusCode> {
    let n = film::Entity::find()
        .count(&conn)
        .await
        .map_err(|_| StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)?;
    Ok(Json(n))
}

fn demo(conn: DatabaseConnection) {
let (builder, films) = Foundry::new(conn.clone()).mount_and_handle::<Film>();
let app: Router = builder.build().merge(
    Router::new()
        .route("/films/count", get(count_films))
        .with_state(AppState { films, conn }),
);
let _ = app;
}
fn main() {}

A transaction is the same: conn.begin() on your connection, outside Ferra. Ferra has no transaction-taking method on Resource<M>.

Cross-references (for the curious reader)

Pointers below trace decisions back to their arbitration. They are not required reading for correct use of the APIs above — every guarantee stated on this page stands on its own.

  • ferra-http.md — the typed-extraction reference, the full RFC 7807 taxonomy, and the Tower layer-ordering diagram. Cross-read it when wiring observability or auth around custom handlers.
  • foundry.md — the router-assembly facade. The composition patterns above attach action routes to a Foundry::build() output.
  • ferra-error-handling.md — the closed ERROR_TYPES URI namespace and the consumer-side error-branching pattern.
  • ferra-core.md §“Time vocabulary” — Date and DateTime (used in the worked example’s release_date field).

Error handling

Every Ferra-served HTTP response that is not a success carries an RFC 7807 problem-details body (Content-Type: application/problem+json). Every body’s type field is a URI from a closed set the framework maintains as a single source of truth.

This page is the reference for that closed set: the URI table, the HTTP status / title / example body for each variant, and the consumer-side branching pattern.

The closed ERROR_TYPES URI set

The framework can emit exactly fifteen type URIs on the wire. Every literal in framework source (and in any consumer crate) MUST appear in this set; a CI gate (cargo run -p xtask --bin error_types_closed) fails the build on any drift.

URIHTTP statusTitleSource
https://ferra.rs/errors/not_found404 Not FoundResource Not FoundFerraError::NotFound (<resource>/<id> not found); FerraError::CollectionNotFound (0.13.0: a collection the caller may not use, <resource> not found, no id)
https://ferra.rs/errors/validation400 Bad RequestValidation ErrorFerraError::Validation (extractor failures: malformed JSON body, unparseable path parameter)
https://ferra.rs/errors/validation_failed422 Unprocessable ContentValidation FailedFerraError::Unprocessable (well-formed body whose values violate #[field(...)] rules — see § Validation failures (422))
https://ferra.rs/errors/conflict409 ConflictConflictFerraError::Conflict (fixed detail); FerraError::ConflictWith (0.13.0: your hook’s HookError::conflict, your detail as given)
https://ferra.rs/errors/internal500 Internal Server ErrorInternal Server ErrorFerraError::Internal
https://ferra.rs/errors/payload_too_large413 Payload Too LargePayload Too Largerequest-body-limit middleware
https://ferra.rs/errors/rate_limited429 Too Many RequestsToo Many Requestsrate-limit middleware
https://ferra.rs/errors/unauthorized401 UnauthorizedUnauthorizedFoundry::with_docs_protected(...); the auth pipeline’s authentication failures (0.8.0 Forging I — absent identity where one is required, and every present-but-invalid token)
https://ferra.rs/errors/forbidden403 ForbiddenForbiddenFerraError::Forbidden (0.8.0 Forging I — an #[authorize] predicate returned false for an identity the framework did establish; see ferra-auth.md § Error responses)
https://ferra.rs/errors/invalid_cursor400 Bad RequestInvalid CursorFerraError::InvalidCursor (0.7.5 Enameling — cursor token failed decode; see pagination.md § Cursor pagination)
https://ferra.rs/errors/unsupported_media_type415 Unsupported Media TypeUnsupported Media TypeFerraError::UnsupportedMediaType (a POST / PUT body whose Content-Type is missing or not JSON)
https://ferra.rs/errors/timeout503 Service UnavailableRequest Timeout Budget ExceededFerraError::Timeout (request budget expired before a repository commit started)
https://ferra.rs/errors/multiple_credentials400 Bad RequestMultiple CredentialsFerraError::MultipleCredentials (0.12.0: a request that presents more than one credential: Authorization, the API key header and the cookie in any combination, and any of them twice; refused before any verification, whatever they hold)
https://ferra.rs/errors/identity_unavailable503 Service UnavailableIdentity UnavailableFerraError::IdentityUnavailable (0.12.0: a credential could not be verified because the identity source is out of reach: the key set of the identity provider could not be fetched with no fresh key cached, or the API key store failed; no Retry-After)
https://ferra.rs/errors/service_unavailable503 Service UnavailableService UnavailableFerraError::ServiceUnavailable (0.13.0: your hook reported, with HookError::unavailable, that something it depends on is out of reach; unlike timeout, it can follow a commit; no Retry-After)

Three of the fifteen URIs (payload_too_large, rate_limited, unauthorized) are emitted by middleware layers, not through FerraError. The framework’s full URI surface is the union of the two paths; both are governed by the same ERROR_TYPES slice. (unauthorized is emitted from both — the docs-protection middleware and, since 0.8.0, FerraError::Unauthorized on the per-operation authorization path.)

The unauthorized (401) and forbidden (403) URIs encode a distinction consumers should branch on rather than collapse. A 401 means the framework could not establish who the caller is: no credential was presented, or the one presented did not validate. A 403 means it established the caller’s identity successfully and the operation’s authorization rule still refused. A 403 is therefore positive evidence that the token was accepted — retrying with fresh credentials will not help, whereas on a 401 it may. Only 401 responses carry WWW-Authenticate: Bearer; a 403 is not an authentication challenge (RFC 9110 §15.5.2 vs §15.5.4).

One refusal is deliberately not a 403: when an IsOwner rule refuses a row that belongs to someone else, the answer is the not_found (404) a missing row gets, byte for byte, so the caller cannot learn that the row exists (see ferra-auth.md § Error responses).

The validation (400) and validation_failed (422) URIs are intentionally distinct. A malformed request body (JSON parse failure, type mismatch on a required field, an Id parameter that will not parse) returns 400 — the request was syntactically unprocessable. A well-formed request body whose values violate the model’s declarative #[field(...)] rules returns 422 — the request parsed cleanly but its semantics were rejected. The split follows RFC 9110 §15.5.1 (400) vs §15.5.21 (422).

Worked example bodies

not_found — 404

Returned by every read / update / delete that resolves to zero matching rows.

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/not_found",
  "title": "Resource Not Found",
  "status": 404,
  "detail": "films/c2bb1f10-72b8-486a-9f2b-c92e4a2cdf41 not found"
}

validation — 400

Returned when an inbound JSON body or a path parameter fails the framework’s typed deserialisation, or when an Id parameter fails to parse. Declarative-rule violations on a well-formed body are the separate 422 path — see § Validation failures (422).

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/validation",
  "title": "Validation Error",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "query parameter `filter[title]` is repeated",
  "errors": [
    { "field": "filter[title]", "code": "duplicate_parameter", "message": "query parameter `filter[title]` is repeated" }
  ]
}

The errors member is one top-level array of {field, code, message}, the same shape as on the 422 path. code is drawn from the closed list in § Validation codes; field is the decoded query parameter, body for a malformed body, or the path parameter’s name.

conflict — 409

Returned when a write would violate a unique constraint (duplicate slug, primary-key collision, etc.). The detail is fixed: the database’s message — which names the constraint and the table — goes to the server log (INFO, target ferra_http::conflict), never to the client.

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/conflict",
  "title": "Conflict",
  "status": 409,
  "detail": "the request conflicts with an existing resource"
}

internal — 500

Returned for any database / infrastructure failure not classifiable as one of the typed variants above. detail is always the constant literal "internal server error" — no internal path fragment, no crate name, no underlying-library substring leaks (constitution §I).

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/internal",
  "title": "Internal Server Error",
  "status": 500,
  "detail": "internal server error"
}

payload_too_large — 413

Emitted when an inbound request body exceeds the framework’s default 1 MiB cap (constitution §I — DoS protection).

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/payload_too_large",
  "title": "Payload Too Large",
  "status": 413,
  "detail": "request body too large"
}

unsupported_media_type — 415

Returned when a POST or PUT body is not declared as JSON: the Content-Type is missing, or is neither application/json nor application/<name>+json (parameters such as charset are ignored). Nothing is read or written.

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/unsupported_media_type",
  "title": "Unsupported Media Type",
  "status": 415,
  "detail": "the request body must be JSON: send `Content-Type: application/json`"
}

timeout — 503

Returned when the configured request budget expires before a Ferra repository commit starts. The unfinished transaction rolls back, and no Retry-After header is sent. Once a commit starts, the handler completes and returns its own response, never this 503; only a model’s after_commit hook is still bounded by the remaining budget, and when it is cut the answer is a 500 internal with the commit standing. See Request time budget.

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/timeout",
  "title": "Request Timeout Budget Exceeded",
  "status": 503,
  "detail": "the request exceeded its time budget; no change was committed"
}

multiple_credentials — 400

Returned when a request presents more than one credential: Authorization, the API key header and the cookie count, in any combination, and any of them sent twice. Presence decides, never validity: the request is refused before any verification, whatever the credentials hold, and the body never names which ones. Send one credential per request. New in 0.12.0.

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/multiple_credentials",
  "title": "Multiple Credentials",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "send one credential per request"
}

identity_unavailable — 503

Returned when a credential cannot be verified because the identity source is out of reach: the key set of the identity provider (JwtConfig::key_set) could not be fetched and no fresh key is cached, or the API key store failed during a lookup. A token that the cached keys cannot verify is a 401 instead, never this. No Retry-After header is sent, and the body never says why: the cause goes to a warn trace. New in 0.12.0.

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/identity_unavailable",
  "title": "Identity Unavailable",
  "status": 503,
  "detail": "the credential could not be verified; retry later"
}

service_unavailable — 503

Returned when a hook of yours returns HookError::unavailable(detail): something the hook depends on (a queue, a payment provider) is out of reach. The detail is yours. No Retry-After header is sent. New in 0.13.0.

After a commit the write stands. The same type answers an unavailable returned by after_commit, which runs once the row is committed: the response is a 503, and the row is written. A client must not retry a non-idempotent request blindly (RFC 9110 § 9.2.2): read the resource first, or send an idempotency key. timeout says the opposite (nothing was committed); identity_unavailable is about the credential, never about your code.

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/service_unavailable",
  "title": "Service Unavailable",
  "status": 503,
  "detail": "the payment provider is not reachable"
}

rate_limited — 429

Emitted by the framework’s default rate-limiter on mutation routes (POST / PUT / DELETE). The response carries a Retry-After header, in whole seconds, never below 1.

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/rate_limited",
  "title": "Too Many Requests",
  "status": 429,
  "detail": "rate limit exceeded"
}

unauthorized — 401

Emitted by Foundry::with_docs_protected(verifier) when an unauthenticated request reaches the docs surface. New in 0.5.0.

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/unauthorized",
  "title": "Unauthorized",
  "status": 401,
  "detail": "authentication required"
}

Every other 401 (missing, malformed, expired or badly signed token, wrong iss or aud, unknown kid) has the same bytes and the headers WWW-Authenticate: Bearer and application/problem+json, whatever the reason, so a caller cannot probe which check failed. Since 0.12.0 its detail is “valid credentials are required to access this resource” (it was “a valid Authorization: Bearer token is required to access this resource”): match on type, not on detail.

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/unauthorized",
  "title": "Unauthorized",
  "status": 401,
  "detail": "valid credentials are required to access this resource"
}

validation_failed — 422

Returned when an inbound POST or PUT body parses cleanly but violates one or more #[field(...)] rules declared on the target model. The full worked example with multi-field aggregation lives in § Validation failures (422); the short form:

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/validation_failed",
  "title": "Validation Failed",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "validation failed",
  "errors": [
    { "field": "title", "code": "min_length", "message": "must be at least 1 character" }
  ]
}

The errors member on this variant is an array of {field, code, message}, field being the wire-side field name — every violation observed during the validation pass is included (no short-circuiting), so a consumer never needs to retry to discover further violations.

Validation failures (422)

A 422 response fires when the request body is well-formed — it parses as JSON and deserialises into the model’s request shape — but one or more values violate the declarative #[field(...)] rules on the target model. Validation runs before persistence on every POST (create) and PUT (update) handler, so an invalid payload never reaches the database. The wire shape is identical across create and update.

This is the 422 path. The 400 validation path above continues to denote extractor failures — a body that does not parse as JSON at all, a path parameter that will not parse as the declared type. Both paths share the application/problem+json envelope and the same errors array; only the codes differ (see § Validation codes).

The model-side declaration grammar — every supported rule, its default English message, and the compile-time FRG-2NN codes that protect typos — is documented in ferra-forge.md § Validation rules. This section pins the wire shape your consumer sees.

Worked example: multi-field violation

For a Film resource declared as:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    #[field(min_length = 1, max_length = 255)]
    pub title: String,
    #[field(min = 0, max = 10)]
    pub rating: i32,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

a request that violates two fields simultaneously:

POST /films HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{ "title": "", "rating": 99 }

receives:

HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "https://ferra.rs/errors/validation_failed",
  "title": "Validation Failed",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "validation failed",
  "errors": [
    { "field": "title",  "code": "min_length", "message": "must be at least 1 character" },
    { "field": "rating", "code": "max",        "message": "must be at most 10" }
  ]
}

Both fields appear in the same response. Ferra never short-circuits on the first failed rule, so a consumer that submits a payload with N invalid fields receives N entries in errors in a single round-trip. Within a single field, every rule that fired produces its own entry — #[field(min_length = 5, email)] on a value of "ab" produces two entries for that field, min_length and email.

Assertion contract for SDK consumers

A consumer driving validation off the wire response asserts the following invariants on a 422:

Wire fieldValueNotes
HTTP status422always equal to the body’s status integer
Content-Type headerapplication/problem+jsonidentical envelope to every other Ferra error
type"https://ferra.rs/errors/validation_failed"pinned URI; closed-namespace member (table above)
title"Validation Failed"distinct from "Validation Error" (the 400 path’s title)
status422 (integer)
detail"validation failed"constant literal — does NOT echo input back into the response (constitution §I — no reflected-XSS on the error path)
errors[{field, code, message}]one entry per rule that fired; field is the wire-side field name (the same name that appears in the request body’s JSON), code is from § Validation codes, message is human-readable English

The field of an entry is the field name of the request body. A field’s JSON name is its Rust name: a serde attribute that renames a model field does not compile (FRG-116, see ferra-forge.md § Field names on the wire).

_links is never present on a 422 body. Validation failure is terminal — there is no resource yet, no self-link to thread, no hypermedia to follow. A consumer that branches on the response’s _links.self.href should treat 422 as the absent-link case.

Update-vs-create symmetry

The validation step runs identically on POST /<resource> and PUT /<resource>/{id}. The 422 body is identical across both. A field omitted from a PUT body is “no change” (Ferra’s existing partial-update semantics) and bypasses that field’s per-field rules. A field present with explicit null on a PUT body for a #[field(required)] Option<T> field fails with the code required — null on the wire is a positive declaration of “set to none”, which the rule rejects.

Consumer-side branching pattern

Add one branch to the existing match on the wire type field:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn on_error(body: &serde_json::Value) {
    match body["type"].as_str() {
        Some("https://ferra.rs/errors/validation_failed") => {
            // 422 path — read body["errors"] as an array of
            // {field, code, message} and surface each entry into your
            // form's per-field error UI; branch on `code`.
        }
        Some("https://ferra.rs/errors/validation") => {
            // 400 path — same `errors` array, other codes.
        }
        // ... other arms ...
        _ => {} // not an error of Ferra's namespace
    }
}
}

Server-side, when handling a FerraError value, the 422 path reads through the new variant:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraError;

fn observe(err: &FerraError) {
    match err {
        FerraError::Unprocessable(_) => {
            // 422 — declarative-rule violation
        }
        FerraError::Validation(_) => {
            // 400 — extractor failure
        }
        // FerraError is #[non_exhaustive]: keep a wildcard arm
        _ => {}
    }
}
}

FerraError::Unprocessable is the typed home for the 422 path; FerraError::error_type returns "https://ferra.rs/errors/validation_failed" on this variant.

Hook errors

A hook returns ferra::hooks::HookError; Ferra turns it into the response, so a hook never builds one. Four constructors:

ConstructorAnswer
HookError::failed(msg)500 internal; msg is logged, never sent
HookError::conflict(detail)409 conflict; your detail is served as given
HookError::unprocessable(field, code, message)422 validation_failed, one error {field, code, message}
HookError::unavailable(detail)503 service_unavailable, your detail

The detail of conflict, unprocessable and unavailable is your text, served as given: put no value in it that the caller may not read. (A conflict from a storage constraint keeps its fixed text, never the database’s message.)

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::ValidationCode;
use ferra::hooks::HookError;

let _ = HookError::failed("the ledger table is locked");
let _ = HookError::conflict("the seat is already booked");
let _ = HookError::unprocessable("amount", ValidationCode::Max, "insufficient balance");
let _ = HookError::unavailable("the payment provider is not reachable");
}

A ? on a FerraError is a 500. A hook that reads another model and propagates its error with ? answers 500 internal with the generic body, whatever the source was (a 403, a 404, a 422): the other model’s status and detail describe a request the caller did not make, and could reveal its rows. Ferra logs the source’s status and type. To answer a 409 or a 422, match the error and build it with the constructors above.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraError;
use ferra::hooks::HookError;

fn read_other_model(found: Result<(), FerraError>) -> Result<(), HookError> {
    found?; // a FerraError here becomes HookError::failed: 500, generic body
    Ok(())
}
let _ = read_other_model;
}

From after_commit the row is already written, so a 409 or a 422 would claim the opposite. failed answers 500, unavailable answers 503, and conflict and unprocessable answer 500 internal. Do not put in a detail a value the caller may not read.

Validation codes

Every entry of errors carries a code from this closed list (ferra::ValidationCode, as_str() is the wire value). Later releases may add codes, never change one.

CodeStatusWhere
invalid_json400the body is malformed or of the wrong shape
invalid_path_param400a path segment cannot be read
duplicate_parameter400a query key Ferra reads is repeated
invalid_parameter400page or per_page is not an integer
not_filterable400filter[x] on a field that is not filterable
not_sortable400sort on a field that is not sortable
unsupported_operator400an unknown filter operator, or a comparison on a non-date field
invalid_filter_value400a filter value of the wrong type
invalid_date400a malformed date filter, or a non-UTC DateTime filter
invalid_pagination400the page and cursor mode rules
unknown_field422a body key outside the write projection
required, min_length, max_length, min, max, pattern, email, url422the #[field(...)] rules
json_too_deep, json_too_large422JSON field bounds
reference_not_found422the parent a foreign key names does not exist or is not usable by the caller; field is the foreign key, one fixed message

ValidationErrors::from_garde_report keeps these codes for a report the derive lowered; a message that does not come from the derive (a garde type of your own) is reported invalid_json.

Consumer-side branching

The recommended consumer pattern is to compare the wire type field against the URI constants — never against the Display form of the error. The URI is the wire contract; the message text is not.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
fn what_to_do(body: &serde_json::Value) -> &'static str {
    match body["type"].as_str() {
        Some("https://ferra.rs/errors/not_found") => "404: the resource is not there",
        Some("https://ferra.rs/errors/validation") => "400: extractor failure",
        Some("https://ferra.rs/errors/validation_failed") => "422: a #[field(...)] rule was violated",
        Some("https://ferra.rs/errors/conflict") => "409: a unique constraint",
        Some("https://ferra.rs/errors/payload_too_large") => "413: split the request",
        Some("https://ferra.rs/errors/rate_limited") => "429: check Retry-After",
        Some("https://ferra.rs/errors/unauthorized") => "401: send a valid token",
        Some("https://ferra.rs/errors/forbidden") => "403: the rule refuses this caller",
        Some("https://ferra.rs/errors/invalid_cursor") => "400: restart from the first page",
        Some("https://ferra.rs/errors/unsupported_media_type") => "415: send application/json",
        Some("https://ferra.rs/errors/internal") => "500: retry with backoff",
        _ => "not an error of Ferra's namespace",
    }
}
}

Server-side, when handling a FerraError value (for example, when mapping to a custom log line or a metrics tag), use the typed FerraError::error_type method:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraError;

fn log_one(err: &FerraError) {
    tracing::warn!(error_type = err.error_type(), "request failed");
}
}

FerraError::error_type returns the URI of each of the eleven variants. Two URIs, payload_too_large (413) and rate_limited (429), reach the wire through middleware layers and are never observed as FerraError values.

OpenAPI schema constraint

The OpenAPI spec the framework emits at /docs/openapi.json constrains ProblemDetails.type to the closed ERROR_TYPES set as an enum. SDK generators (orval, openapi-generator, kiota, …) produce a typed union over the eight URIs rather than a free-form string — consumers in TypeScript, Go, Python, etc. branch exhaustively on the wire type value.

For an AI coding assistant generating client code: the type field is an enum, not a free-form string. Synthesising a value outside the eight URIs above fails OpenAPI schema validation against the spec.

Observability events

Two structured tracing events fire alongside the wire surface of the error namespace and the deprecation surface. Both follow the <snake-cased crate name>::<event segment> target convention so an operator can filter them independently via tracing-subscriber’s EnvFilter (RUST_LOG=ferra_http::sunset=warn, etc.).

TargetLevelTriggerDocumented at
ferra_http::rate_limitWARNevery 429 emission from the governor middlewarethis file § “rate_limited — 429”
ferra_http::sunsetWARNonce per (version, sunset) per process when a request lands past the declared sunset datefoundry.md § “Post-sunset warn-event”

The post-sunset event carries five fields (version, sunset, days_overdue, http.method, http.target); the rate-limit event carries three (http.method, http.target, http.retry_after_seconds). Both event-schemas are contracts under ADR-0015 §“event schema is a contract” — additive widenings only, never renames. In both, http.target is the request path: the query string never reaches these events (ADR-0076).

When the observability Cargo feature is on, the framework ALSO advances a metrics::counter! named ferra.sunset.post_sunset_hits on every post-sunset hit (regardless of the once-per-process dedup that gates the warn-event). See foundry.md § “Post-sunset warn-event” for the full surface.

Adding a new URI

The framework’s URI namespace is closed by design: a new variant requires a coordinated change across three surfaces.

  1. Add the URI literal to ERROR_TYPES in crates/ferra-core/src/error.rs.
  2. Extend the OpenAPI emitter so ProblemDetails.type carries the new value in its enum constraint (the emitter reads ERROR_TYPES directly; this step is automatic once step 1 lands).
  3. Publish at least one HTML anchor on https://ferra.rs/errors/<variant> returning HTTP 200, so that AI agents and human readers reach a stable documentation page for the new variant.

The release-blocking CI gates verify (1) source-side closure (error_types_closed) and (3) network-side resolution (uri_resolution_probe, both xtask binaries). New variants without all three gates green fail the build.

The closed-namespace contract is recorded in ADR-0026. The contract is not load-bearing for consumer correctness — the URI table above is self-contained.

Deploying to Lambda with Neon

The complete application and OpenTofu template are in examples/lambda-neon. It uses Lambda Web Adapter 1.1.0, an arm64 image, and Neon’s pooled PostgreSQL endpoint. GET /live is unauthenticated and performs no database or secret-store access. Use /live, not /ping, as the adapter readiness path.

Lazy connections in a frozen execution environment

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use std::time::Duration;
use sea_orm::{ConnectOptions, Database, DatabaseConnection, DbErr};

async fn connection(url: &str) -> Result<DatabaseConnection, DbErr> {
    let mut options = ConnectOptions::new(url);
    options.connect_lazy(true).max_connections(2).min_connections(0)
        .connect_timeout(Duration::from_secs(10))
        .acquire_timeout(Duration::from_secs(10))
        .test_before_acquire(true)
        .max_lifetime(Duration::from_secs(300))
        .idle_timeout(Duration::from_secs(60));
    Database::connect(options).await
}
}

Construction performs no network connection. A request can fail while Neon is resuming; a subsequent acquisition reconnects. Two connections bound each execution environment’s pool; the maximum across concurrent Lambda environments still needs to fit the database’s capacity. test_before_acquire detects a connection closed while the environment was frozen.

Use the Neon connection string whose hostname includes -pooler. The pooler uses transaction mode: protocol-level prepared statements are supported when its prepared-statement tracking is enabled. Do not rely on LISTEN/NOTIFY, SET or other session state, session advisory locks, SQL PREPARE/DEALLOCATE, or WITH HOLD cursors. Ferra’s guarded writes use one transaction and one server connection. The operator canary verifies these properties on the real Neon service; the ordinary test suite exercises PostgreSQL directly.

Server-side timeouts on the application role

A Lambda environment can be frozen right after a 503 timeout: the dropped transaction’s ROLLBACK then waits for the thaw, and the transaction keeps its locks and a pooler server connection. Bound it on the server, once, for the role the application connects as:

ALTER ROLE CURRENT_USER SET statement_timeout = '27s';
ALTER ROLE CURRENT_USER SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '30s';

statement_timeout sits just above the request budget (24 s). Below it, Postgres would cancel a statement Ferra is still waiting for and the client would get a 500 internal instead of the 503 timeout; above it, the budget answers first, and the server timeout only reaps a statement left running by a frozen environment. idle_in_transaction_session_timeout closes a session left idle inside a transaction. Role settings apply when a session starts, so they reach the pooled endpoint, where a session-level SET does not hold; they apply to new sessions only. The operator canary must confirm that Neon accepts ALTER ROLE CURRENT_USER SET for the application role before relying on these bounds.

Limits and secrets

Configure FerraLayer::new().no_rate_limit() and API Gateway throttling instead: Ferra’s limiter has a separate bucket in each Lambda execution environment. The template sets burst 20 and rate 10 requests per second. Configure a body limit of 5,500,000 bytes, below Lambda’s synchronous 6 MB event limit, and a request budget of 24 seconds: the first data request also waits up to 4 seconds for secret loading, and 24 + 4 stays below the template’s 29-second API Gateway integration timeout, so the client gets Ferra’s 503 timeout, not a gateway 504. The function timeout is 30 seconds. A started database commit is awaited rather than canceled, and the after_commit hook after it is bounded by the remaining budget (a 500 when cut, the commit standing); the raw connection escape is outside the rollback guarantee.

Keep DATABASE_URL and JWT_SECRET in SSM Parameter Store SecureString parameters. The template carries only their names and ARNs. The operator sets the values separately, so credentials never enter OpenTofu state or Lambda configuration. The example reads them through the Parameters and Secrets extension’s local endpoint with the temporary AWS session token; it never logs those values or that token.

The extension is available during INVOKE, not INIT. The example starts /live first and initializes the cached Ferra router on the first data request with retryable OnceCell::get_or_try_init. Secret loading has its own bounded startup wait; the request budget governs the initialized Ferra handlers. The first invocation’s total time and the container extension’s installation must be measured by the operator canary. Do not wrap writes in an unconditional outer timeout, which could cancel a commit already in progress. See AWS’s extension lifecycle.

OpenTofu walkthrough

  1. Create Neon outside OpenTofu; choose the pooled connection string. Create the example table and the role’s timeouts with examples/lambda-neon/schema.sql.
  2. Create the two SSM SecureString values with your secret-management tooling.
  3. In examples/lambda-neon/infra, run tofu init, then tofu apply with deploy_function=false to create the image repository and execution role.
  4. Build and push the arm64 image using the README instructions. Copy the extension layer files into the image; the Dockerfile requires the extracted layer directory.
  5. Set image_digest to the pushed digest and run tofu plan, then tofu apply with deploy_function=true. Set spa_origin to your one HTTPS SPA origin.
  6. Check /live, authenticated CRUD and restore, JSON refusals, descending cursors, and the optional slow route. Record cold start, memory, image size, idle cost, and the first-request initialization in the canary journal.

AWS deployment and its costs require the operator’s accounts and remain a manual acceptance step. The canary feature should be disabled in production images.

Stability policy

What a Ferra release guarantees, what may change between 0.9 and 1.0, and how to upgrade. It applies from v0.9.0.

How Ferra is released

  • One version for the whole workspace, one git tag per release: v0.9.0, v0.9.1, v0.10.0. Nothing is published on crates.io.

  • An application depends on a tag, and on the facade only:

    ferra = { git = "https://github.com/ferra-rs/ferra", tag = "v0.13.1" }

  • A tag is never moved. CHANGELOG.md has one section per tag.

What the contract is

The contract is what the ferra crate exports, and nothing else:

  • the FerraModel derive and its attributes (#[ferra(...)], #[field(...)], #[authorize(...)], #[behavior(...)]), with the FRG- code of each refusal;
  • Foundry, FoundryBuilder and their options;
  • JwtConfig and its types; the FerraIdentity trait; testing::bearer;
  • Id, DateTime, Date, Time;
  • the error types, and the problem+json documents they render — status, type URI, title;
  • ferra::hooks: FerraHooks, Saving, Saved, Committed, HookTx (with HookTx::system), TxResource, SystemAccess, and HookError, what an application’s hook returns to refuse a write;
  • for a route of your own: Resource, ResourceHandle, CollectionQuery, CursorQuery, Page, CursorPage, FerraPath, FerraJson, FerraAuthLayer, the two middlewares, CurrentUser;
  • the description of a model, to read: meta, model;
  • the Cargo features observability and test-support;
  • the HTTP behavior of the generated routes: paths, methods, statuses, the shape of bodies and of the OpenAPI document.

The exact list, name by name, is api/ferra.txt; the signatures are in the other files of api/.

Not in the contract, whatever its visibility:

  • the implementation crates taken directly (ferra-core, ferra-db, ferra-forge, ferra-http, ferra-openapi): depend on ferra;
  • everything #[doc(hidden)] — the __private modules, the constructors of the meta types, ferra::ferra_core, ferra::ferra_http, FerraDraft, NoHooks, Hooked, ApplyDraft, FerraHooksDeclared, FerraSystemOnly, FerraNotBlameable, FerraSystemGrant and HookRunner, the write transaction WriteTx of ferra-db and its entry points (begin, commit, lock_row, insert_row, update_row, delete_row, soft_delete_row, restore_row, lock_parent_shared), and the retry switch FoundryBuilder::retry_switch of the test-support feature, which only Ferra’s own tests set. It exists for the derive’s generated code and for Ferra’s own crates, and changes without notice;
  • the code the derive generates: read it with cargo expand, do not call it;
  • the text of a log event, of a detail member, of a compiler diagnostic beyond its FRG- code;
  • the inside of a cursor: it is an opaque string, hand it back as it came.

The repository is not in the contract

Since 0.10.0 the repository (PgRepository, FerraRepository, DatabaseTransaction, FerraDbError) and FerraState are not exported: a route of your own reaches a model’s rows through Resource<M>, which applies the model’s rules. See migrating-to-0.10.md.

What a version number means

Ferra is 0.x: it follows Semantic Versioning as Cargo reads it for 0.x.

From → toMay it break the contract?What you do
v0.9.0 → v0.9.1 (patch)No. Fixes and additions only.Change the tag.
v0.9.x → v0.10.0 (minor)Yes, each break listed in CHANGELOG.md under “Changed — breaking”, with what to do.Read the changelog, change the tag, follow the compiler.
v0.x → v1.0.0Yes, for the last time without a major bump.Same.

Two exceptions, both written in the changelog when they happen:

  • A security fix may change behavior in a patch release — a request that was wrongly served is refused. Refusing more is never held back for a minor.
  • Becoming more permissive is not a break. A 400 that becomes a 200 (a filter on a date field, a descending cursor walk), a new optional attribute, a new variant of a #[non_exhaustive] enum, a new method on Resource, a new field on a meta type, a new member in a response object: all are additions (a client ignores members it does not know).

A removed attribute keeps a migration diagnostic for at least one minor version: the compiler says what to write instead (as FRG-105, FRG-106 and FRG-335 do for what 0.9.0 removed).

Third-party crates in the contract

Types of other crates appear in Ferra’s signatures, and two crates are re-exported whole. A major version change of one of them is a break of Ferra, made in a minor release and listed in the changelog.

CrateWhere you meet itIn 0.9.x
axumFoundry::build() returns an axum::Router; extractors, middlewares0.8
Sea-ORMferra::sea_orm, whole; the entity derives; DatabaseConnection2.x
gardeferra::garde, whole; ValidationErrors::from_garde_report0.23
tower-httpFerraLayerBuilder::cors, trace_layer0.7
secrecyJwtConfig::single_secret takes impl Into<SecretString>0.10
serdeevery model derives it1
uuidConditionType is implemented for uuid::Uuid: a Uuid column is a Field<M, Uuid> (ADR-0070)1

What ferra::sea_orm and ferra::garde contain is theirs, under their own version numbers: Ferra’s snapshots do not cover it, and no tool can see inside a re-export. Four things stand in for that:

  • Five of them are exact requirements. garde, utoipa-scalar, jiff, tower-http and base64 are declared =x.y.z in Ferra’s manifests. If your application also names one of them, it must name the same version (or a requirement that version satisfies): another patch fails to resolve. A patch of one of them, for an advisory for instance, reaches you in a Ferra patch release.
  • Sea-ORM is a public dependency of Ferra. A new major version of Sea-ORM (or a new minor of garde, a 0.x crate) is a breaking change of Ferra: it ships in a minor release, and the changelog says so.
  • Your sea-orm follows Ferra’s major. The documented way to use Sea-ORM is to declare sea-orm yourself, at the major version the release you use was built with. Each release’s changelog names it and gives the line to change in your Cargo.toml. A different major is two copies of the crate; #[derive(FerraModel)] refuses it with FRG-400, and cargo tree -d -i sea-orm shows it. Declaring no sea-orm and writing ferra::sea_orm::… is supported as well.
  • A gate pins it. reexport_pin fails CI when the lockfile holds two copies of either crate, or another version than the one documented here; changing the pin is a decision made in one change with this page and the changelog.

Sea-ORM in Ferra’s signatures

Ferra’s own signatures name a Sea-ORM type in four places only:

  1. the ferra::sea_orm re-export and the prelude’s glob of its entity prelude;
  2. the constructors that take the application’s connection, Foundry::new(DatabaseConnection) and api_key::PgApiKeyStore::new(DatabaseConnection), and the DatabaseConnection re-export;
  3. the trait bounds that make a model a Sea-ORM entity (Mountable’s, the builder’s, Resource’s, HookTx::resource’s and SystemAccess’s where clauses: ModelTrait, EntityTrait, ActiveModelTrait, ActiveModelBehavior, FromQueryResult, IntoActiveModel, IntoValueTuple, PrimaryKeyTrait), and PkValue<M>, the key type the entity declares;
  4. the trait impls that make a Ferra value type (Id, Date, DateTime, Time) a Sea-ORM column (feature sea-orm of ferra-core).

The rule for later lots: no other Ferra-owned signature names a Sea-ORM type. That covers hooks, authority, actions, computed fields, the request context and resource access: they take and return Ferra’s types (FerraError, Resource<M>). Your own code reaches Sea-ORM through your own DatabaseConnection, outside Ferra’s contract.

The gate sea_orm_surface reads api/*.txt and fails on any other line that names sea_orm::. The internal items of ferra-db (PgRepository, FerraRepository, FerraDbError, WriteGuard) are not in the facade; the gate lists them apart.

Rust version

  • The minimum supported Rust version is 1.94, checked in CI. Raising it is allowed in a minor release, never in a patch, and is listed in the changelog.
  • The repository pins the toolchain it is developed with (rust-toolchain.toml); an application is free to use a newer one.
  • Ferra builds and tests natively on Linux, macOS and Windows. What is proven: a real trial on Windows 11 on 2026-09-30, before lot L4, built the workspace, ran both test suites and check_compile_error_spans there. The checklist L4.28 runs it again on the final state of the lot, with a default clone; until it has passed, the claim rests on that first trial.

What is planned, and will not break you

Each of these is an addition under the rules above: an external authenticator next to .with_auth (RS256/JWKS, sessions); PATCH; relations; a response envelope for custom routes.

How the contract is kept

Four gates block CI (CONTRIBUTING.md has the commands):

  • public_api_snapshot — the public API of each crate is a text file under api/. Any difference fails until the snapshot is regenerated and committed with the change, which makes every change of the contract visible in review.
  • semver_checks — cargo-semver-checks compares each crate with the previous tag: a break without the minor version bump that allows it fails.
  • sea_orm_surface — fails when a line of api/ names sea_orm:: outside the places listed in “Sea-ORM in Ferra’s signatures”.
  • reexport_pin — ferra::sea_orm and ferra::garde are the crates themselves, and neither of the two gates above can see inside a re-export: this one fails when Cargo.lock holds two copies of either, or a version other than the documented one (Sea-ORM 2.x, garde 0.23.x).

And one test names the contract item by item (crates/ferra/tests/contract_surface.rs), so that removing one breaks the build on the stable toolchain too.

Migrating from 0.13 to 0.14

0.14.0 (Riveting) removes declarations that read as a restriction and restricted nothing. Each entry below is a change that can stop a 0.13 application from compiling; read the entries, then update the application’s git dependency to v0.14.0. CHANGELOG.md lists every change.

groups is a compile error (FRG-137)

Before. #[ferra(groups = [...])] on a field, and groups = [...] inside projection(...), compiled. Ferra parsed the key and dropped it: the field was served on every read and accepted in the default write body, whatever the list, the empty list groups = [] included. A password hash declared with #[ferra(groups = [])] was served to every caller allowed to read the model.

After. The key is refused whatever its value, on a field, inside projection(...) and on the struct, with FRG-137, spanned on the groups key. FieldMeta::groups (ferra_core::meta::FieldMeta) is removed: it was always empty. FRG-306 (skip next to a non-empty groups) is retired with it.

Migration. Replace groups with what Ferra enforces:

You wrote groups to…Write instead
keep a field out of every response and write body#[ferra(skip)]
accept a field on write and never serve it (a password)#[ferra(write_only)]
choose the fields of a shaperead = [...] and write = [...] on a projection(...), see Projections and routing
serve or accept a field only to some callers#[field(read = …)] and #[field(write = …)], see Authentication and Authorization
 
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "users")]
#[ferra(auth = "bearer")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    #[ferra(write_only)]
    pub password_hash: String,
    #[ferra(skip)]
    pub internal_notes: String,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}

Code that reads FieldMeta::groups (a loop over meta().fields) no longer compiles: delete the loop. The slice was empty for every field, so the loop never ran.

A Ferra attribute where the derive does not read it is a compile error (FRG-138)

Before. The derive declares the helper attributes ferra, field, behavior, operation and authorize, so the compiler accepted each of them on the struct and on every field, and Ferra read each in one place only. A #[field(owner)] written on the struct marked no field as the owner; an #[authorize(...)] or #[behavior(...)] written on a field declared nothing. The model compiled, and the declaration did nothing.

After. Each of these is refused with FRG-138, spanned on the attribute path:

You wroteWhere it goes instead
#[field(...)] on the structon the field it describes
#[authorize(...)] on a fieldon the struct; a rule for one field is #[field(read = …, write = …)]
#[behavior(...)] on a fieldon the struct
#[operation(...)] on a fieldnowhere: add the route yourself with .route(...), see Custom handlers

Migration. Build, and move or remove each attribute the compiler points at. A model that carried a struct-level #[field(owner)] had no owner field: check that the rows are still protected as you meant, then put #[field(owner)] on the column that holds the owner.

#[ferra(hooks)] on a system_only model is a compile error (FRG-135)

Before. A #[ferra(system_only)] model is a table that only a system grant writes (see System grant). It could declare #[ferra(hooks)] and an impl FerraHooks. It compiled, and the hooks never ran: the model serves no write, and a grant inserts into it without running its hooks.

After. The hooks key on a system_only model is refused with FRG-135, spanned on hooks, as a write rule on it already was. The hooks of a grant are those of the model that declares the grant, never the target’s.

Migration. Delete hooks and the impl FerraHooks from the system_only model. That code never ran, so nothing is lost. If it was meant to write an entry into the model, move it to the impl FerraHooks of the model whose writes it records, and call tx.system().insert(..) there:

#[ferra(system_only)]                                   // the log model: no `hooks`, no `impl FerraHooks`
#[ferra(auth = "bearer", hooks(system = log::Model))]   // the hooked model: it owns the hooks and the grant

promotes_from off a default projection, or malformed, is a compile error (FRG-316)

Before. promotes_from compiled on a projection without default = true, where it was read and dropped, and with any string as its value, "v1" or the name of a projection that does not exist included. Only the presence of the key was checked, and only next to default = true.

After. FRG-316 refuses promotes_from on a projection without default = true, spanned on the key, and a value that is neither "auto-derived" nor "named:<name>" with <name> another projection declared in the same model (never the projection itself), spanned on the value. The value is still not checked against repository history: a former named default that you removed in the same change can no longer be named; write "auto-derived".

Migration. Remove promotes_from from a projection that is not the default. Write the value of a promoted projection as "auto-derived", or as "named:" followed by the name of a projection the model declares.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
#[ferra(projection(name = "v1", read = [id, title]))]
#[ferra(projection(
    name = "v2",
    default = true,
    promotes_from = "v1",
    breaking_change_version = "0.2.0",
    read = [id, title],
))]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
    pub id: i32,
    pub title: String,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
pub enum Relation {}
impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
#![allow(unused)]

use ferra::FerraModel;
use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, FerraModel, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "films")]
#[ferra(auth = "none")]
#[ferra(projection(name = "v1", read = [id, title]))]
#[ferra(projection(
    name = "v2",
    default = true,
    promotes_from = "named:v1",
    breaking_change_version = "0.2.0",
    read = [id, title],

    pub title: String,

#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, EnumIter, DeriveRelation)]
